name: Protecting Humanity Through Law in War and Peace

exam.label: Wed 2 Dec · 09:00–12:00 · USC
exam.rules: Closed book, in person, three hours (Wed 2 Dec, 09:00–12:00, New USC). You may bring Blackstone's International Law Documents, a print-out of Heinsch's ICL Reader, the Geneva Conventions, APs I and II, and human rights treaties — clean copies only: highlighting allowed, no notes, tabs only with treaty names. Dictionaries allowed. Relevant ICL, IHL and IHRL instruments are also uploaded in ANS.
exam.format: Part A: two essays, chosen from three options (i)–(iii) — answer exactly two, 30 points each, max 750 words each. Analytical and discursive: the examiners want critical engagement, graded on a slider (structure, depth, argument, insight, use of materials), not issue points. Part B: one compulsory problem question on a fictional scenario combining several course themes, with discrete sub-questions asking for legal advice; 40 points, max 1,000 words. Always cite the legal provisions; extra credit for jurisprudence and impactful scholarship (cite in brackets).
template: Budget the three hours: about 50 minutes per essay and 70 minutes for the problem, plus reading time. Answer exactly two essays.
Problem: answer each sub-question under its own heading. Start by classifying the situation (peace, IAC, NIAC, internationalised, occupation) with the test and the facts.
Then the applicable law: which IHRL treaties, and does jurisdiction reach extraterritorially (spatial, personal, functional)? Which IHL rules? Any valid derogation?
Per right or rule: state the IHRL test and the IHL test and how they co-apply (lex specialis versus harmonious interpretation, Hassan, GC 36 para 64). Use the facts' own words.

Individual criminal responsibility where relevant: which crime (contextual plus specific elements), mode of liability (Arts 25, 28), and the forum (ICC Arts 12–13, 17, 27, 127; universal jurisdiction).

Essays (750 words): a one-sentence thesis, three or four arguments each anchored in a case, provision or reading, a counter-argument, and a critical conclusion (humanity, effectiveness, fragmentation, selectivity).
Cite in brackets (ANS doesn't allow footnotes): article numbers always; cases and authors for extra points.

topics.title: Humanity in international law
core: Humanity has two senses: humankind (the collective) and humaneness (a quality of conduct, compassion and restraint), as in Coupland, IRRC 2001. Both shape IL: 'crimes against humanity' versus 'principles of humanity'.

The Martens Clause (1899 Hague Preamble; API Art 1(2)): in cases not covered, civilians and combatants remain under the principles of international law derived from established custom, the principles of humanity and the dictates of public conscience. Meron reads it as interpretive guidance and a source of pressure for custom, not an independent source (Nuclear Weapons AO para 87).
'Elementary considerations of humanity' (Corfu Channel; Nicaragua para 218) are a source of obligation independent of treaty. CA3 is a 'minimum yardstick'.
The humanization of IHL (Meron 2000): the human rights influence on IHL, the expansion of NIAC rules (Tadić Jurisdiction), and the move from State-centric reciprocity to individual protection.

The individual moved from object to subject: rights holders (IHRL), duty bearers (ICL: 'crimes against IL are committed by men, not by abstract entities', IMT). Peters calls this 'Humanity as the A and Ω of sovereignty'; Teitel's 'Humanity's Law'.

Hostis humani generis (enemy of mankind, the pirate) versus hostia humani generis (Bikundo: the victim offered up in humanity's name, exemplary justice). This is a critical reading of ICL's selectivity.
Critical views: Urueña says 'humane' is a contested normative standard, open to power and exclusion. Decolonising humanity: who defines it, and the colonial origins of IHL.
Humanity links to jus cogens and erga omnes obligations: the prohibitions of genocide, torture, CAH and slavery, and the basic rules of IHL (Wall para 157: 'intransgressible').

Coupland proposes a working definition: humanity 'arises from and signifies restraining the capacity for armed violence and limiting its effects on security and health'. On this view humanity is the 'lowest common denominator' of most of international law, not just IHL and IHRL: the UN Charter and arms control restrain violence for national security, IHRL protects personal security, and IHL 'stands in the middle' (personal security while national security is being decided by force).

Coupland argues that 'humanity-sentiment' (humaneness) is the counterweight to inhumanity, so crimes against humanity are crimes against humanity-humankind committed through acts of inhumanity. He wants to move humanity out of its 'ambiguous' natural-law corner into the domain of health, where the effects of armed violence can be measured and evidenced. Critical use: this makes humanity objective and universal, but risks reducing a normative idea to measurable harm.

Meron's limits on the Martens Clause: it 'does not allow one to build castles of sand'. Except in extreme cases, the principles of humanity and dictates of public conscience cannot by themselves make a weapon or method unlawful. Its real effects are elsewhere: it pushes customary law to rest on opinio juris rather than battlefield practice, weakens reciprocity, gives NGOs a lever, and argues against a non liquet. He doubts it has had any influence on the battlefield itself.

Van Beers, Corrias and Werner identify three paradoxes in 'enemy of mankind' language: humanity transcends State sovereignty yet empowers States to exercise extraordinary (universal) jurisdiction; it places individuals outside normality yet requires recognising their legal personality; it claims universality yet depends on particular cultural and political understandings. They reject both naive enthusiasm and sceptical dismissal: invoking humanity is never innocent, because it empowers, legitimises, includes and excludes.

Bikundo's thesis is that ICL 'embodies the international community through iconic presentation'. The phrase hostis humani generis does two things: it supplies jurisdiction where there would be none, and it dehumanises whoever it is applied to. Given the geographic selectivity of cases, the claim that 'humanity sits in judgment over inhumanity' is better put as one segment of humanity judging another ('selective universality'): the accused become scapegoats, the judges sovereigns.
lecture: Lecture 1 frames 'humanity as subject' with open questions: does it have concrete meaning, or is it irrelevant or imperialistic? Context of deployment is key — Koskenniemi: concepts of humanity or dignity 'take a completely different color, depending on the political project of those invoking the terms'. Does it assume natural law? Is it a general principle of (international) law? Does humanity have 'enemies'?

Martens Clause: 1899 text, 'populations and belligerents remain under the protection and empire of the principles of international law, as they result from the usages established between civilized nations, from the laws of humanity, and the requirements of the public conscience'; the 1907 text reads 'inhabitants and the belligerents' and 'the dictates of the public conscience'. Pictet (1956): 'the principle of humanity stands out on its own … all other principles hang from it'.

What the Martens Clause does (Lecture 2): rejects 'not prohibited means permitted'; keeps protection alive in gaps; links interpretation to public conscience. Nuclear Weapons AO: the Martens Clause 'has proved to be an effective means of addressing the rapid evolution of military technology' (para 78); it belongs to the rules of API that were already custom when adopted, reaffirmed in API Art 1(2) (para 84); its 'continuing existence and applicability is not to be doubted', as an affirmation that IHL principles apply to nuclear weapons (para 87). The 'functional validity … objective barrier' wording on the Lecture 2 slide does not appear anywhere in the Court's opinion (paras 1–105), so don't quote it as the ICJ's words. Its function remains disputed: interpretive principle, source of law, or catalyst for new rules.

1977 version (API Art 1(2)): 'usages established among civilized peoples' became 'established custom', 'laws of humanity' became 'principles of humanity', and the clause moved from a preamble into an operative article. Stronger institutionally, but 'established custom' may narrow one route for legal development.
1949: humanity centred on the protected person. Common Article 3 is the minimum in NIAC; protection attaches to human beings, not only reciprocity.

Humanity at a crossroads: ICRC President Spoljaric to the UNSC on the 'disregard for our shared humanity'. In Sept 2024 the ICRC and six States (Brazil, China, France, Jordan, Kazakhstan, South Africa) launched the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to IHL. About 120 States joined, with seven workstreams (prevention, national IHL committees, IHL and peace, civilian infrastructure, hospitals, ICT, naval warfare) and a leaders' statement at UNGA80 on 21 Sept 2025. The High-Level Conference to Uphold Humanity in War meets in Amman, Jordan on 7 Dec 2026 and is expected to adopt a political declaration, not a new treaty or mechanism. Question posed: can humanity mobilise commitment without becoming vague or selectively invoked?

Human dignity's foundations: Judeo-Christian thought (the person as 'someone, not something'), Kant (dignity as autonomy), Pico della Mirandola, Schiller ('give him food and shelter … dignity will follow'). In adjudication, 'thin' dignity just restates the catalogue of rights; 'thick' dignity is a substantive value of its own.

Humanity as the engine of ICL (Lecture 3): Jackson at Nuremberg ('abnormal and inhuman conduct'; 'civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated'); Rome Statute preamble ('atrocities that deeply shock the conscience of humanity'); IMT: crimes are 'committed by men, not by abstract entities'.

Main IHL principles listed by Heinsch: distinction, prohibition of attacking persons hors de combat, prohibition of indiscriminate attacks, proportionality, prohibition of unnecessary suffering, humanity, military necessity. Hague law (means and methods) versus Geneva law (protection of persons hors de combat).

cases.name: Corfu Channel
cases.holding: Albania's duty to warn rested on 'elementary considerations of humanity, even more exacting in peace than in war'.
cases.use: Humanity as a source of obligation outside treaty.

cases.name: Legality of Nuclear Weapons AO
cases.holding: The cardinal principles of IHL are distinction and the prohibition of unnecessary suffering. The Martens Clause is an effective means of addressing rapid technological change. Fundamental IHL rules are 'intransgressible'.
cases.use: The Martens Clause; the principles of humanity; new weapons (and AI later).

cases.name: Tadić (Jurisdiction Appeal)
cases.holding: 'A State-sovereignty-oriented approach has been gradually supplanted by a human-being-oriented approach.' Customary war crimes exist in NIAC (paras 97, 134).
cases.use: The humanization narrative.

cards.q: What does the Martens Clause say, and what is its legal status?
cards.a: Where there are gaps, persons remain protected by custom, the principles of humanity and the dictates of public conscience. Its status is contested: at minimum an interpretive aid that closes the 'everything not prohibited is permitted' gap; on a bolder view, an autonomous source (Meron is cautious).

cards.q: What are Coupland's two meanings of humanity?
cards.a: Humankind, the collective human race, and humaneness, the quality of compassion and restraint in behaviour. IL protects the first through the second.

cards.q: What is Bikundo's 'hostis' versus 'hostia humani generis'?
cards.a: From the enemy of mankind (the pirate, an outlaw) to the sacrificial victim. ICL selects exemplary defendants and punishes them in humanity's name, a critique of its selectivity and theatre.

cards.q: Give three examples of 'humanity' operating as law.
cards.a: The Martens Clause; elementary considerations of humanity (Corfu Channel); crimes against humanity; jus cogens and erga omnes protections; the CA3 minimum yardstick.

cards.q: How did the Martens Clause change between 1899 and API Art 1(2) (1977)?
cards.a: 'Usages established among civilized peoples' became 'established custom'; 'laws of humanity' became 'principles of humanity'; 'populations and belligerents' became 'civilians and combatants'; it moved from the preamble into an operative article. Institutionally stronger, but 'established custom' may exclude emerging usages.

cards.q: What did the ICJ say about the Martens Clause in Nuclear Weapons?
cards.a: It is 'an effective means of addressing the rapid evolution of military technology' (para 78); like other API rules that were already custom, it was reaffirmed in API Art 1(2) (para 84); its 'continuing existence and applicability is not to be doubted', and it affirms that IHL principles apply to nuclear weapons (para 87). Note: the 'functional validity … objective barrier' wording on the Lecture 2 slide is not in the Court's opinion.

cards.q: Thick versus thin conceptions of human dignity?
cards.a: Thin: dignity is a shorthand for the catalogue of human rights. Thick: dignity is an independent substantive value that can ground new rights or limit State action (e.g. Kantian autonomy).

cards.q: What is Coupland's definition of humanity, and why does it widen the field?
cards.a: Humanity 'arises from and signifies restraining the capacity for armed violence and limiting its effects on security and health'. So not only IHL and IHRL but also the UN Charter, self-defence rules and arms control 'promote humanity'; IHL sits between national security (arms control) and personal security (IHRL). Humanity becomes the 'lowest common denominator' of international law (Coupland 2001, pp 986–988).

cards.q: What does Meron mean by 'castles of sand' (Martens Clause)?
cards.a: The clause cannot, alone and except in extreme cases, delegitimise weapons or methods of war. It helps interpretation, argues against a non liquet, tilts custom towards opinio juris and away from reciprocity, and empowers NGOs. New prohibitions are better reached through distinction, proportionality and unnecessary suffering than by stretching the clause (Meron 2000, pp 87–88).

cards.q: What are van Beers et al's three paradoxes of 'humanity' in ICL?
cards.a: (1) It transcends sovereignty yet empowers States to exercise extraordinary jurisdiction; (2) it puts individuals outside normality yet must recognise their legal personality (and dignity, even of the perpetrator); (3) it claims universality yet rests on particular cultural and political understandings. Hence the question of auctoritas: who decides what humanity means?

excerpts.text: In cases not covered by this Protocol or by other international agreements, civilians and combatants remain under the protection and authority of the principles of international law derived from established custom, from the principles of humanity and from the dictates of public conscience.
excerpts.why: Humanity as a source or interpretive principle: the narrow, middle and broad readings (Meron, Cassese).

topics.title: Actors, obligations and peacetime frameworks
core: There is a tripartite typology of State obligations: respect (negative), protect (positive, against third parties: due diligence, Osman test of knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk), and fulfil (provide).
Human rights obligations have an objective, non-reciprocal character (Mégret). Erga omnes partes in treaties; interstate complaints (ECHR Art 33; CAT Art 21).
IHL binds all parties to an armed conflict, including non-state armed groups (CA3; APII). Common Article 1 (respect and ensure respect) creates internal and external dimensions.
ICL obligations between States: aut dedere aut judicare (CAT Art 7, the Grave Breaches regime), universal jurisdiction, and cooperation with courts (Rome Part 9).

Non-state actors (Clapham): armed groups bound by IHL (and arguably IHRL where they control territory). Corporations have no direct treaty obligations: UNGPs (protect, respect, remedy), domestic civil liability (Vedanta, Okpabi), and the draft business and human rights treaty.
Individuals are duty bearers under ICL, while under IHRL the State is the duty bearer.

Limitations: an interference is lawful if (1) prescribed by law, (2) pursues a legitimate aim, and (3) is necessary in a democratic society (pressing social need, proportionality, margin of appreciation). Abuse of limitations to silence opposition is caught by Art 18 ECHR (Navalny v Russia; Merabishvili).

Derogation (ICCPR Art 4; ECHR Art 15): a public emergency threatening the life of the nation, officially proclaimed and notified; measures strictly required by the exigencies; consistent with other IL obligations; non-discriminatory. Non-derogable rights include life (except lawful acts of war under ECHR Art 15(2)), torture, slavery, non-retroactivity, plus the core of fair trial (HRC GC 29).
Absolute rights: the prohibition of torture and ill-treatment can't be limited or derogated from (Mavronicola: absoluteness means no justification, even when the threat is grave). Link to jus cogens.
The normalisation of emergency in counter-terrorism (SR report A/HRC/37/52): permanent emergencies, vague definitions, abuse against civil society.

Mégret frames the 'special character' of human rights obligations as a clash of form and function, quoting Craven: the treaty form suggests rights-holders are merely 'fortuitous beneficiaries' of a contract between States, while the regime's purpose is quasi-constitutional. Taken to its extreme, ratification is 'declaratory of states' obligations rather than constitutive of them', and human rights obligations become the typical erga omnes obligations, justifying routine scrutiny of other States without any injury of one's own.

Earliest authorities for the special character of human rights treaties: ICJ, Reservations to the Genocide Convention AO (1951) para 23: the parties 'do not have any interests of their own', only a common interest, so there is no 'perfect contractual balance'; and a State can become a party despite objections to its reservation (para 24). European Commission, Austria v Italy (Pfunders, 1961): ECHR obligations are 'essentially of an objective character'. Consequence for invalid reservations: severability, so the State stays bound without the reservation (Loizidou v Turkey; Belilos).

Withdrawal from human rights treaties. Where there is a denunciation clause (ECHR Art 58, ACHR Art 78, CERD Art 21), it has rarely been used: Greece left the ECHR 1969–74 after the coup, Trinidad and Tobago denounced the ICCPR Optional Protocol and the ACHR (1998–99), Venezuela the ACHR (2013), and none had retroactive effect. Where there is none (ICCPR), HRC General Comment 26 (after North Korea's 1997 attempt) says the Covenant implies no right of denunciation and its protection 'devolves with territory'. Mégret calls this the unique 'stickiness' of human rights commitments, in contrast with Rome Statute Art 127.

Clapham identifies five pressures that make non-state actors a human rights problem: globalisation, privatisation, fragmentation, feminisation and criminalisation. Privatisation 'relabels' the same act: what was a human rights violation becomes a tort or breach of contract, and the private actor can invoke competing rights of its own. Criminalisation shows international law already binds non-state individuals, and he sees 'no convincing conceptual reason' why it should not extend to corporations and rebel groups as such.

Clapham on armed groups: the ICRC position is that non-state armed groups generally have no IHRL obligations, except where they exercise de facto State-like authority, and even then speaks only of 'responsibilities' (Breitegger). Clapham replies that each of Sivakumaran's seven routes explaining why armed groups are bound by IHL (ratification by the State, domestic law, treaties binding third parties, consent to CA3, claims to represent the State, exercising State-like functions, custom) could equally ground IHRL obligations.

Counter-view (Bantekas and Oette): extending human rights obligations to outlawed non-state actors such as terrorist groups risks making States 'irresponsible', because it shrinks the State's positive duty to prevent and punish into a merely negative one. Criminal law handles such conduct better. They accept complementary obligations for corporations, and conclude that armed groups uphold rights only through their own internal processes, a 'cherry-picking' that breeds uncertainty and lets States blur their own commitments. Alston (on the Tamil Tigers): no ICCPR obligations, but the UDHR's 'common standard of achievement' applies to any group that aspires to represent a people.

Rebel groups and human rights (Bantekas and Oette): CA3, APII and API Art 1(4) address armed groups directly, and ARSIWA Art 10(2) (the conduct of a successful insurrectional movement is attributed to the new State) can be read as giving rebels obligations even before they take power. Rebel human rights obligations are strongest where they control territory, since the territorial State cannot protect people there, and are reinforced by SC resolutions addressed to insurgents. Below the armed-conflict threshold rebels are treated like terrorist groups, without human rights obligations. Illustration: the CPP-NPA's internal purges in the Philippines (Oplan Missing Link, 1988), where victims of torture by their own comrades found no forum.
lecture: Tension: IHRL is a branch of PIL, built on sovereignty and consent, yet it constrains sovereignty. Human rights treaties are 'special': States bind themselves to other States but create rights for individuals (Mégret).

IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-2/82 (Effect of Reservations): human rights treaties 'are not multilateral treaties of the traditional type … for the reciprocal exchange of rights'; States assume obligations 'towards all individuals within their jurisdiction'. Loizidou: the ECHR is an 'instrument of European public order'. Erga omnes obligations originate in Barcelona Traction.

Respect, protect, fulfil. Protect means proactively ensuring persons do not suffer violations, a due diligence duty prominent in violence against women (Velásquez Rodríguez v Honduras). 'Doing nothing is not an option.'
IHL: who is bound, and do its rules create individual rights? Context and status are key (hostilities or occupation; civilian, combatant or POW).

Common Article 1 with Pictet's gloss: respect for the Conventions is asserted 'as much because of the respect one has for it oneself as because of the respect one expects from one's opponent'. Nicaragua v Germany (ICJ) as the live example.

Grave breaches enforcement: GCI Art 49 (GCII 50, GCIII 129, GCIV 146, API): enact penal sanctions, search for alleged offenders 'regardless of their nationality', try or hand over, with fair-trial safeguards.
ICL: what is its purpose — justice, accountability, punishment? Supranationality, aut dedere aut judicare, cooperation and arrest warrants, States parties versus non-parties, groups.

Lecture 4 (Peace): interdependence and indivisibility. Vasak's 'generations' are no longer a useful construct; indivisibility is accepted in principle but delivery differs. Two-track realisation: essential and immediate versus progressive. Emergence of solidarity rights. Absolute versus non-absolute rights, shaped by jus cogens.

Reservations: VCLT Art 2 definition; must not defeat object and purpose (Art 19(3)). Given indivisibility, many human rights reservations are questionable. HRC General Comment 24: no reservations to core guarantees such as the right to a remedy; reservations must be specific, transparent, refer to a specific provision, and not be general. Example: Qatar's reservation to ICCPR Art 3 and the objections to it.

Limitations define a right's scope; they are built into specific clauses (ICCPR Arts 18(3), 19(3)). Margin of appreciation adds a pluralist element but defers to States, controversially where there is no global consensus.

Five headings for assessing a limitation: prescribed by law (accessible, foreseeable, precise — Republican Party of Russia v Russia 2011); legitimate aim (exhaustive and narrowly construed list); necessary in a democratic society (pluralism, tolerance, broadmindedness — democracy is not majority rule); pressing social need; proportionality (if a less severe measure would do, the restriction fails).

Abuse of limitations: Navalnyy v Russia (GC 2018) under Art 18 ECHR. Merabishvili v Georgia: restrictions can pursue a plurality of purposes; Art 18 is violated where the ulterior purpose is predominant.

cases.name: Osman v UK
cases.holding: Under Art 2 a State has a positive obligation to take reasonable operational measures where authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to an identified individual's life from third parties.
cases.use: The duty to protect, a due diligence standard.

cases.name: Lawless v Ireland / A and Others v UK
cases.holding: An emergency threatening the life of the nation is a wide margin for the State. In A v UK, indefinite detention of foreign terror suspects only was disproportionate and discriminatory, despite a valid derogation.
cases.use: Review of derogation measures; non-discrimination.

cases.name: Navalny v Russia (GC)
cases.holding: Repeated arrests at protests pursued the ulterior purpose of suppressing political pluralism, a violation of Art 18 together with Arts 5 and 11.
cases.use: Abuse of permissible limitations.

cards.q: What is the three-step test for limiting a qualified right?
cards.a: Prescribed by law (accessible and foreseeable), a legitimate aim, and necessary in a democratic society (proportionate, least restrictive), within the margin of appreciation.

cards.q: What are the conditions for a valid derogation?
cards.a: A public emergency threatening the life of the nation; official proclamation and notification; measures strictly required by the exigencies; consistent with other IL obligations; non-discriminatory; non-derogable rights are untouched.

cards.q: What does Common Article 1 require?
cards.a: To respect and ensure respect for the Conventions in all circumstances: internally (one's own forces and population) and externally (not encouraging, aiding or assisting violations by others, and taking feasible steps to bring them to an end, per the ICRC 2016 Commentary).

cards.q: How are corporations bound in the protection of humanity?
cards.a: Indirectly: States' duty to protect (CESCR GC 24), UNGP soft law (the responsibility to respect, human rights due diligence), the OECD Guidelines, domestic tort litigation, and ICL for individuals within companies (Lundin trial).

cards.q: Why are human rights treaties described as 'special' (OC-2/82)?
cards.a: They are not reciprocal exchanges of rights between States; their object is protecting individuals irrespective of nationality, so States assume obligations towards all individuals within their jurisdiction. This explains, e.g., the treatment of reservations and erga omnes partes standing.

cards.q: What does HRC General Comment 24 say about reservations?
cards.a: Reservations incompatible with object and purpose are invalid; core guarantees (e.g. the right to a remedy, peremptory norms) cannot be reserved; reservations must be specific and transparent and refer to particular provisions. The HRC claims competence to assess validity and to sever invalid reservations.

cards.q: Merabishvili's contribution to Art 18 ECHR?
cards.a: A restriction may pursue several purposes, some legitimate and some not. Art 18 is violated where the illegitimate (ulterior) purpose was predominant, assessed on all the circumstances.

cards.q: Clapham versus Bantekas and Oette: should armed groups have human rights obligations?
cards.a: Clapham: yes. The routes that bind armed groups to IHL (Sivakumaran's seven) work equally for IHRL; UN COIs, SC resolutions and truth commissions already demand it; we must question who the duty-bearers are (ch 28, pp 571–578). Bantekas and Oette: be careful. Making outlawed groups duty-bearers lets States off their positive duties; criminal law is the better tool, though rebels controlling territory should answer for fundamental rights (ch 19, pp 1430, 1467).

cards.q: Can a State withdraw from the ICCPR?
cards.a: No, according to HRC General Comment 26 (1997, after North Korea tried): the Covenant has no denunciation clause and is not the type of treaty that implies one; its rights 'belong to the people' and devolve with territory, whatever changes in government. The UN Secretary-General as depositary agreed. Mégret calls this 'stickiness'; contrast ECHR Art 58 and Rome Statute Art 127.

cards.q: What are Clapham's five pressures, and what does 'relabelling' mean?
cards.a: Globalisation, privatisation, fragmentation (armed groups, international organisations), feminisation (private violence against women) and criminalisation. Relabelling: once a public function is privatised, the same harm is treated as a tort or contract breach, not a human rights violation, and the private actor can raise its own rights (e.g. property in a privatised shopping centre, Appleby v UK).

topics.title: Armed conflict: classification and co-application
core: IAC (CA2): any resort to armed force between States, with no intensity threshold (Tadić para 70; ICRC Commentary). It includes total or partial occupation, even without resistance. API Art 1(4) covers wars of national liberation.

NIAC (CA3): protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups, or between such groups (Tadić para 70). Two criteria: intensity (number, duration and intensity of clashes, weapons, casualties, displacement, SC involvement) and organisation (command structure, ability to carry out operations, discipline, ability to implement IHL; Haradinaj, Boškoski). APII has a higher threshold: territorial control, and the State must be a party.

Internationalised NIAC: a foreign State's intervention on the side of the armed group, or overall control by a State over the group (Tadić Appeals para 137), turns it into an IAC. 'Transnational' conflicts with non-state actors across borders (e.g. against ISIS) are generally treated as NIAC.
Conflicts can transform (from internal disturbances to NIAC to IAC). Classification may be mixed or 'parallel' in the same territory (Nicaragua para 219).

Co-application: IHRL continues in armed conflict (Nuclear Weapons para 25; Wall para 106: some rights only IHRL, some only IHL, some both; DRC v Uganda para 216). For the right to life, IHL as lex specialis determines what is 'arbitrary' (para 25).
Lex specialis is increasingly questioned (Milanovic's 'lost origins': it originally meant harmonious interpretation, not displacement). Duffy shows the trend of courts adjudicating co-applicability.
Hassan v UK (2014): in an IAC, Art 5 ECHR is read in harmony with GCIII and GCIV internment powers, without a formal derogation, keeping the safeguards of review and non-arbitrariness.

Introduction to targeting: distinction (API 48), the definition of military objectives (API 52(2): by nature, location, purpose or use, effective contribution to military action and definite military advantage), proportionality (51(5)(b)), precautions (57), prohibition of superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering (35(2)), indiscriminate weapons.

Bantekas and Oette argue IHL is best seen not as a system of rights but as protection of 'protected persons': its humanisation is influenced by human rights but should be kept apart from rights talk. Human rights answer the power imbalance between a State and those it governs; IHL rests on the reciprocal expectations of equal sovereigns (and self-interest). Rules such as the bans on indiscriminate attacks or denial of quarter cannot be enforced by their beneficiaries in battle, and IHL is premised on a permission to kill those taking a direct part in hostilities.

Bantekas and Oette read the ICJ's lex specialis (Nuclear Weapons para 25; Wall para 106) as a conflict-of-norms rule, not a tool of interpretation: where an IHL rule truly cannot be reconciled with a human rights rule, IHL prevails. Critics say this artificially fragments the two bodies of law. The HRC (GC 31 para 11: 'complementary, not mutually exclusive') and the Inter-American Commission (using VCLT Art 31(3)(c), each body interpreted in the light of the other) take the harmonising view.

Why human rights bodies rarely apply IHL directly (Bantekas and Oette): their mandate is limited to their own treaty, they lack IHL expertise, they risk acting ultra vires and colliding with ICL case law, and accepting lex specialis would mean admitting their own treaty is subordinate. So they translate IHL into human rights terms. In Chechnya (Isayeva, Yusupova and Bazayeva) and south-east Turkey (Ergi) the ECtHR accepted that lethal force against insurgents could be justified but required feasible precautions to minimise incidental civilian loss, mirroring API Art 57. Unlike IHL, this duty binds only the government side.
lecture: Three theories of the IHL–IHRL relationship (Heinsch): strict separation (IHL in war, IHRL in peace), complementarity, and convergence (cumulative application for the most effective protection). UN Secretary-General's Bulletin 1999: 'cumulative application of all norms which protect the individual'.

History of co-application: Tehran Human Rights Conference 1968, Res XXIII ('peace is the underlying condition for the full observance of human rights and war is their negation'); the ICRC delegate: the UDHR and the Geneva Conventions 'are both derived from one and the same ideal'.

Authorities for co-application: Wall AO para 106 (three situations); ILC Fragmentation Study Group 2006 (norms bearing on one issue should be interpreted to give a single set of compatible obligations); 30th International Red Cross Conference, Res 3 (2007).

The gap in internal disturbances: the ICRC definition (a serious confrontation with violence but no armed conflict) means IHL does not apply, only IHRL subject to derogation. The Turku Declaration (1990) on minimum humanitarian standards tried to fill it, with little success.

IHL is non-derogable: built for extreme situations, it already balances military necessity and humanity. IHRL's non-derogable core: life, torture, slavery, imprisonment for contractual debt, recognition before the law, non-retroactivity, freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

Protected persons: IHL protects categories (combatants, civilians, wounded and sick, POWs); IHRL protects all human beings within jurisdiction (HRC GC 31: territory, jurisdiction, power or effective control, including forces abroad; some bodies add direct and foreseeable impact). Central tension: universality versus jurisdiction as a threshold.

Why classification matters (examples: Iran, Ukraine, Gaza): it determines the applicable law. IAC: GCs I–IV, API, weapons treaties, customary IHL. NIAC: CA3, APII, customary IHL, and IHRL as gap filler. Below the threshold: national law and IHRL.

cases.name: Tadić (Jurisdiction and Appeals)
cases.holding: Defined armed conflict and NIAC (protracted armed violence plus organised groups), and set the overall control test for internationalising a conflict.
cases.use: The classification test in every problem question.

cases.name: Wall AO
cases.holding: The protection of human rights conventions does not cease in armed conflict. There are three possible situations (some rights exclusively IHL, some exclusively IHRL, some both). The ICCPR, ICESCR and CRC apply extraterritorially in occupied territory.
cases.use: Co-application; extraterritoriality.

cases.name: Hassan v UK (GC)
cases.holding: Detention of an Iraqi in an IAC was compatible with Art 5 when read in light of IHL internment powers, even though the UK had not derogated, provided there were safeguards against arbitrariness.
cases.use: Harmonious interpretation; detention.

cases.name: Haradinaj / Boškoski
cases.holding: Indicative factors for intensity (seriousness of attacks, spread, mobilisation, weapons) and organisation (headquarters, command, logistics, ability to negotiate and speak with one voice).
cases.use: Applying the NIAC threshold to facts.

cases.name: Isayeva, Yusupova and Bazayeva v Russia; Ergi v Turkey
cases.holding: In NIAC-type operations (missile attack on a civilian convoy in Chechnya; an ambush operation in Turkey), the use of lethal force against insurgents could be legitimate, but Art 2 was violated because the State did not take feasible precautions in choosing means and methods to avoid or minimise incidental loss of civilian life, nor investigate effectively.
cases.use: How human rights courts import IHL-type precautions and proportionality into Art 2 without applying IHL; co-application in NIAC.

cards.q: Tadić definition of armed conflict?
cards.a: Armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between States, or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a State.

cards.q: What are the two NIAC criteria, and the factors for each?
cards.a: Intensity: frequency and gravity of attacks, weapons, casualties, displacement, SC attention. Organisation: command structure, headquarters, capacity to plan and execute operations, discipline and ability to implement IHL, negotiation capacity.

cards.q: How does an internal conflict become international?
cards.a: Through direct intervention of another State's troops, or a foreign State's overall control over the armed group (Tadić: financing, equipping plus coordinating or helping plan operations).

cards.q: What is Milanovic's critique of lex specialis?
cards.a: Its origins are about interpretation, not hierarchy. Courts use it loosely; it doesn't explain which rule prevails. Better to reason through harmonious interpretation and norm conflict avoidance.

cards.q: What are the three situations in the Wall para 106?
cards.a: Some rights may be exclusively matters of IHL, some exclusively of IHRL, and others matters of both, in which case IHL is lex specialis.

cards.q: Name the three theories of the IHL–IHRL relationship.
cards.a: Strict separation (IHL for war, IHRL for peace); complementarity (they complement each other); convergence (cumulative application of all protective norms, UNSG Bulletin 1999). Today's mainstream: co-application with harmonious interpretation (Wall para 106; ILC Fragmentation 2006).

cards.q: What are 'internal disturbances and tensions', and which law applies?
cards.a: Serious confrontations with violence that do not reach NIAC (APII Art 1(2) excludes riots and sporadic violence). IHL does not apply; IHRL applies, subject to derogation, plus domestic law. The Turku Declaration (1990) proposed minimum humanitarian standards to fill the gap.

cards.q: Why do human rights courts apply 'IHL through the back door' rather than IHL itself?
cards.a: Their mandate covers only their own treaty; applying IHL directly risks ultra vires findings, clashes with ICL case law and an admission that IHL overrides their treaty (lex specialis). So they read Art 2 to require precautions and proportionality in military operations (Isayeva; Ergi). Effect: in NIAC, human rights procedures give victims far stronger remedies than IHL (Bantekas and Oette, pp 1268–1270).

excerpts.cite: ICTY Appeals Chamber, Decision on Jurisdiction (1995), para 70
excerpts.text: …an armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between States or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organized armed groups or between such groups within a State.
excerpts.why: The classification test: IAC on any resort to force; NIAC needs intensity and organisation.

topics.title: Occupation
core: Art 42 of the Hague Regulations: territory is occupied when actually placed under the authority of the hostile army. The test is effective control: foreign forces able to exert authority, without the sovereign's consent, and the sovereign unable to exercise its authority (Armed Activities para 173; ICTY Naletilić). The GCIV regime applies from first contact for persons (the Pictet functional approach).

The end of occupation is debated. A 'functional approach' (Gaza: Israel kept control of the land, sea and air borders, restrictions on movement of people and goods, collection of import and export taxes and military control over the buffer zone, so its obligations remain commensurate with its effective control: OPT AO 2024 paras 93–94).

Art 43 of the Hague Regulations: the occupant must restore and ensure, as far as possible, public order and safety (French text: 'l'ordre et la vie publics', so 'public order and civil life' on slide 11), respecting the laws in force unless absolutely prevented. It administers the territory for the benefit of the local population and gains no sovereignty (OPT AO 2024 para 105); it is only administrator and usufructuary of the hostile State's public immovable property (Hague Regulations Art 55).

GCIV protections: prohibition of forcible transfers and deportations (Art 49(1)), prohibition of transferring the occupant's own population (Art 49(6), settlements), prohibition of collective punishment (33), destruction of property only if absolutely necessary (53), provision of food and medical supplies (55–56), relief (59), assigned residence and internment for imperative security (78).

Annexation is prohibited by the ban on acquiring territory by force; GCIV Art 47 adds that annexation cannot deprive protected persons of the Convention's protection. In the 2024 OPT AO, prolonged occupation is not unlawful per se (its length 'does not in itself change its legal status', para 109); Israel's continued presence is unlawful because of its sustained abuse of its position through annexation, an assertion of permanent control and the frustration of self-determination (paras 261–262): Israel must end its presence as rapidly as possible, evacuate settlers and make reparation; other States must not recognise or aid.

IHRL in occupation: human rights treaties apply to acts done in the exercise of jurisdiction abroad, particularly in occupied territories (Wall paras 107–113; Armed Activities para 216). Al-Skeini (2011) grounded ECHR jurisdiction on the UK's exercise of public powers and its soldiers' authority and control over individuals (para 149), not on effective control of an area. There is debate over whether IHRL is primary for law enforcement (policing) and IHL for hostilities (Lubell). Dinstein emphasises the IHL framework as primary but complemented by IHRL.

Use of force in occupied territory: the law enforcement paradigm (IHRL) for policing, the conduct-of-hostilities paradigm only where hostilities resume. Detention under GCIV 78 with review. Cultural property (1954 Hague Convention and protocols).
Self-determination: prolonged occupation denies the right of peoples to self-determination, an erga omnes obligation (Wall para 155; Chagos; 2024 AO).

Bantekas and Oette: occupation sits 'between war and peace' and is chiefly governed by IHL, so the full armoury of human rights is not automatically transplanted. But the occupant 'becomes the government responsible' for the territory, not an interim administrator stripped of responsibility, and it may treat inhabitants as lawful targets only if renewed violence reaches the threshold of armed conflict; otherwise its duties resemble human rights in a strained peace. Note that the occupation treaties speak of 'guarantees', not rights.
lecture: Occupation in five steps (Heinsch): (1) Hague Regs Art 42 threshold — territory actually placed under the hostile army's authority, only where it is established and can be exercised; (2) effective control in practice — foreign forces present without valid consent, displacing the local government and able to act in its place; (3) no fighting or declaration needed (CA2(2): even without armed resistance); (4) duties follow control (Hague Regulations Art 43: restore and ensure public order and civil life, respecting existing laws unless absolutely prevented); (5) annexation does not remove protection (GCIV Art 47).

2016 ICRC Commentary: effective control is the main characteristic, but it does not require exercising full authority — the capacity to exercise it suffices; occupation persists despite resistance or temporary loss of parts of the territory.

Occupation without boots on the ground? ICTY Naletilić & Martinović (2003, paras 217–218): sufficient forces present or able to deploy within a reasonable time. The ability to invade alone is not occupation.

Gaza: the 2005 withdrawal did not end all obligations. OPT AO 2024 paras 91–94: continuous physical presence is not decisive; Israel retained powers over borders, movement, taxation and the buffer zone, so its obligations remain commensurate with its effective control (functional approach). The central question: what authority survives withdrawal, and which duties follow?

GCIV structure: general protection of the whole population (Arts 13–26); protected persons' common provisions (general clause Art 27; specific prohibitions Arts 31–34: no coercion, no measures causing physical suffering or extermination, no collective punishment, intimidation or terrorism, pillage, hostage-taking); aliens in a party's territory (Arts 35–46); occupied territories (Arts 47–78); internment rules (Arts 79–135).

Art 27 GCIV: respect for persons, honour, family rights, religion, manners and customs; humane treatment; protection against violence, insults and public curiosity; special protection for women against rape and indecent assault; no adverse distinction.

Internment thresholds: aliens in a party's own territory only if the security of the Detaining Power makes it 'absolutely necessary' (Arts 41–42); in occupied territory only for 'imperative reasons of security' (Art 78), as a measure of last resort with review.

cases.name: Legal Consequences of Israel's Policies in the OPT AO
cases.holding: Israel's continued presence in the OPT is unlawful (11 votes to 4) because of annexation and an assertion of permanent control and the frustration of self-determination (para 261). Israel must end its presence as rapidly as possible, cease all new settlement activity, evacuate all settlers and make reparation. All States must not recognise the situation or aid or assist in maintaining it (12 votes to 3). Its legislation and measures breach CERD Art 3 (para 229). In Gaza its obligations remain commensurate with the effective control it retains (para 94).
cases.use: Prolonged occupation; the functional approach; third-State duties.

cases.name: Armed Activities (DRC v Uganda)
cases.holding: Uganda was an occupying power in Ituri because it substituted its own authority for that of the Congolese government. It was responsible for failing to prevent looting and violations by others, and IHRL applied in occupied territory.
cases.use: The effective control test; occupant's obligations; co-application.

cases.name: Wall AO
cases.holding: Settlements breach GC IV Art 49(6), which also covers measures to organise or encourage transfers (para 120). The wall's route gives expression to those illegal measures, severely impedes self-determination (para 122) and breaches human rights such as freedom of movement and the rights to work, health and education (para 134). Human rights treaties apply in occupied territory (paras 107–113).
cases.use: Occupation and human rights; settlements.

cards.q: When is territory occupied? (Art 42 of the 1907 Hague Regulations)
cards.a: 'Territory is considered occupied when it is actually placed under the authority of the hostile army. The occupation extends only to the territory where such authority has been established and can be exercised.' The test is effective control (Lecture 6, slide 11): foreign forces are present without valid consent, prevent the local government from exercising its authority, and can exercise authority in its place. In Armed Activities (ICJ 2005, para 173) Uganda occupied Ituri because its forces had 'substituted their own authority for that of the Congolese Government'.

cards.q: What does Art 43 of the 1907 Hague Regulations require of the occupant?
cards.a: Once the authority of the legitimate power has in fact passed to it, the occupant 'shall take all the measures in his power to restore, and ensure, as far as possible, public order and safety, while respecting, unless absolutely prevented, the laws in force in the country'. The authentic French text says 'l'ordre et la vie publics', which is why the slides (Lecture 6, slide 11) say 'public order and civil life'. Slide 11's point: these duties follow from control; they are a consequence of occupation.

cards.q: How did the ICJ apply Art 43 in Armed Activities (DRC v Uganda, 2005)?
cards.a: Para 178: as occupying Power in Ituri, Uganda's Art 43 obligation 'comprised the duty to secure respect for the applicable rules of international human rights law and international humanitarian law, to protect the inhabitants of the occupied territory against acts of violence, and not to tolerate such violence by any third party'. Para 179: Uganda was responsible both for its own forces' acts and for any lack of vigilance in preventing violations by other actors in the occupied territory, including rebel groups acting on their own account.

cards.q: Does occupation require fighting, a declaration or recognition?
cards.a: No. Common Art 2(2) of the Geneva Conventions: they apply to all cases of partial or total occupation 'even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance'. Occupation depends on facts, not formal recognition (slide 11). 2016 ICRC Commentary (slide 14): effective control does not require exercising full authority; the mere capacity to exercise it suffices, and occupation can exist despite resistance or temporary loss of parts of the territory.

cards.q: Can there be occupation without troops on the ground?
cards.a: Establishing occupation and maintaining it are different questions (slide 15). Naletilić & Martinović (ICTY Trial Chamber, 31 March 2003, paras 217–218): sufficient forces present OR the capacity to deploy within a reasonable time to enforce authority; the ability to invade alone is not occupation. OPT AO (2024) paras 91–92: physical presence is not indispensable; the decisive criterion is whether authority 'has been established and can be exercised'.

cards.q: Is Gaza still occupied after the 2005 withdrawal? (OPT AO 2024)
cards.a: Israel's withdrawal 'has not entirely released it of its obligations under the law of occupation' (para 94). It remained capable of exercising, and continued to exercise, key elements of authority: control of the land, sea and air borders, restrictions on movement of people and goods, collection of import and export taxes, and military control over the buffer zone, 'even more so since 7 October 2023' (para 93). Its obligations remain 'commensurate with the degree of its effective control' (para 94).

cards.q: Does occupation transfer sovereignty to the occupant?
cards.a: No. Occupation 'is a temporary situation to respond to military necessity, and it cannot transfer title of sovereignty to the occupying Power', and the occupant 'bears a duty to administer the territory for the benefit of the local population' (OPT AO 2024, para 105). Under Art 55 of the Hague Regulations it is only 'administrator and usufructuary' of the hostile State's public buildings, real estate, forests and agricultural estates. Annexation of occupied territory is unlawful (OPT AO para 175), and under GC IV Art 47 annexation cannot deprive protected persons of the Convention's protection (slide 11).

cards.q: Does a prolonged occupation become unlawful because of its length?
cards.a: No. 'The fact that an occupation is prolonged does not in itself change its legal status under international humanitarian law' (OPT AO 2024, para 109). Its legality is judged by the prohibition of the use of force, including the acquisition of territory by force, and by self-determination. Israel's presence is unlawful because of its 'sustained abuse … of its position as an occupying Power, through annexation and an assertion of permanent control … and continued frustration of the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination' (para 261; operative para 285(3), 11 votes to 4).

cards.q: What did the 2024 OPT AO require of Israel and of other States?
cards.a: Israel: end its unlawful presence as rapidly as possible (para 267); immediately cease all new settlement activity (para 268) and evacuate all settlers (para 270); make reparation: restitution, compensation and/or satisfaction (paras 269–271). All States: do not recognise as legal the situation arising from the unlawful presence and do not render aid or assistance in maintaining it (para 279; operative para 285(7), 12 votes to 3); States parties to GC IV must ensure Israel's compliance with it (para 279).

cards.q: Settlements and displacement: which GC IV rules apply?
cards.a: Art 49(6): 'The Occupying Power shall not deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies.' It also covers measures to organise or encourage such transfers (Wall AO para 120; OPT AO paras 115, 119). Art 49(1): individual or mass forcible transfers and deportations of protected persons are prohibited 'regardless of their motive'; Art 49(2) allows only temporary evacuations if the security of the population or imperative military reasons so demand. OPT AO para 147: Israel's policies in Area C breach Art 49(1).

cards.q: Which core GC IV protections apply to protected persons? (slides 19–21)
cards.a: Art 27: respect for their persons, honour, family rights, religious convictions and practices, manners and customs; humane treatment; protection against violence or threats, insults and public curiosity; women specially protected against rape, enforced prostitution and indecent assault; no adverse distinction (race, religion, political opinion). Arts 31–34: no physical or moral coercion (31); no measures causing physical suffering or extermination (32); no collective punishment, intimidation, terrorism or pillage (33); no hostage-taking (34).

cards.q: What must the occupant provide to the population? (GC IV)
cards.a: Art 55: to the fullest extent of the means available to it, ensure the food and medical supplies of the population, bringing them in if local resources are inadequate. Art 56: medical and hospital services, public health and hygiene. Art 59: if the population is inadequately supplied, the occupant 'shall agree to relief schemes' and facilitate them by all the means at its disposal. Art 53: destroying property is prohibited except where 'rendered absolutely necessary by military operations'.

cards.q: Internment under GC IV: aliens versus occupied territory?
cards.a: Aliens in a party's own territory: internment or assigned residence only if the security of the Detaining Power makes it 'absolutely necessary' (Art 42), with reconsideration by a court or administrative board and review at least twice a year (Art 43). Occupied territory: only 'for imperative reasons of security', and then 'at the most' assigned residence or internment (Art 78), by a regular procedure with a right of appeal and periodical review, if possible every six months (slide 24).

cards.q: Do human rights treaties apply in occupied territory?
cards.a: Yes. They apply to acts done in the exercise of jurisdiction outside a State's territory, 'particularly in occupied territories' (Armed Activities para 216; Wall AO paras 107–113; OPT AO para 99), and their protection does not cease in armed conflict (Wall para 106). Under the ECHR, Al-Skeini (2011) para 138 recognises effective control of an area as one basis of jurisdiction, but the UK's jurisdiction in Basra rested on its assumption of public powers and its soldiers' authority and control over the individuals killed (para 149).

cards.q: Which paradigm governs an occupant's force against a demonstrator?
cards.a: Law enforcement under human rights law (the right to life; HRC General Comment 36; McCann v UK): lethal force only when strictly necessary to protect life. The conduct-of-hostilities paradigm applies only where hostilities with an organised armed group have resumed. The syllabus lists this (use of lethal force) as an example of how the frameworks operate in occupation (Lubell; Dinstein).

excerpts.text: Territory is considered occupied when it is actually placed under the authority of the hostile army. The occupation extends only to the territory where such authority has been established and can be exercised.
excerpts.why: Occupation is a question of fact: effective control, not a declaration.

excerpts.text: …the Court will need to satisfy itself that the Ugandan armed forces in the DRC were not only stationed in particular locations but also that they had substituted their own authority for that of the Congolese Government.
excerpts.why: Substitution of authority: Uganda occupied Ituri, so it was responsible for failing to protect there (Art 43).

excerpts.why: The legality of an occupation itself, assessed through jus ad bellum and self-determination.

They are also under an obligation not to render aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by Israel's illegal presence…

mindmap.title: The law of occupation
mindmap.blurb: Eight branches and 41 topics, each with its authorities and key quotes. Includes recall mode and search.

topics.title: Extraterritorial jurisdiction
core: Human rights treaties apply to persons 'within the jurisdiction' of the State (ECHR Art 1; ICCPR Art 2(1) 'within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction', read disjunctively by the HRC in GC 31 para 10 and the ICJ in the Wall).

Spatial model: effective control over an area, through its own forces or a subordinate local administration (Loizidou; Cyprus v Turkey; Ilaşcu; Al-Skeini para 138; Ukraine and Netherlands v Russia for eastern Ukraine from 2014).

Personal model: State agent authority and control over an individual: custody (Öcalan, Al-Saadoon), diplomatic and consular agents, and the exercise of public powers (Al-Skeini sets out the principles at paras 133–137: para 135 public powers exercised with the territorial State's consent; para 136 use of force by agents bringing the individual under their control; para 137 'divided and tailored'. It applies them at para 149: the UK assumed some public powers of a sovereign government and responsibility for security in south-east Iraq, so 'through its soldiers engaged in security operations in Basrah' it exercised authority and control over those killed). Rights can be 'divided and tailored' (Al-Skeini para 137).

Functional and impact model: control over the enjoyment of a right. HRC GC 36 para 63: persons whose right to life is impacted by a State's activities in a direct and reasonably foreseeable manner. IACtHR OC-23/17 on transboundary environmental harm (the State of origin has effective control over activities causing harm). The CRC applied it in Sacchi v Argentina et al. (jurisdiction yes, but inadmissible for non-exhaustion).

The ECtHR was restrictive: Banković (NATO bombing of Belgrade, no jurisdiction, the ECHR's 'legal space') and Georgia v Russia II (2021: no jurisdiction during the 'active phase of hostilities', the 'context of chaos', though jurisdiction existed in the occupation phase); critics said this resurrected Banković. But Ukraine and the Netherlands v Russia (GC decision of 30 Nov 2022) held that Georgia II 'cannot … be seen as authority for excluding entirely … a specific temporal phase of an international armed conflict' (para 558) and that Banković's rejection of 'divided and tailored' rights is 'no longer an accurate statement' (para 571). The merits judgment (9 July 2025) found Russia's planned military attacks across Ukraine 2014–2022 'wholly at odds with any notion of chaos', so those affected were within its jurisdiction through State agent authority and control.

Carter v Russia (2021, the Litvinenko poisoning): a targeted killing by State agents abroad gave jurisdiction through physical power and control over the victim's life ('isolated and specific act'). Contrast this with Georgia v Russia II.

Ukraine and Netherlands v Russia (GC admissibility decision delivered 25 Jan 2023; GC merits 9 July 2025, unanimous): Russia had effective control over separatist areas from 11 May 2014 (military presence, decisive influence, political and economic support), and the separatists' acts are attributable to it. Jurisdiction also covers the post-24 Feb 2022 military attacks: Georgia (II)'s 'context of chaos' did not apply to extensive, planned attacks. Merits: administrative practices of killings, torture including rape, unlawful detention, forced labour, persecution, looting and destruction, and transfer of children, 11 May 2014 – 16 Sept 2022. MH17: Arts 2 (substantive and procedural), 3 (next of kin) and 13. Art 2 interpreted in harmony with IHL.

Surveillance: Wieder and Guarnieri v UK (2023): interception of communications in the UK of persons abroad falls within jurisdiction (the interference occurs in the UK territory), an expansive approach for Art 8.
States push back (US, Israel, UK): the treaty text is territorial, fear of over-stretch to military operations abroad, and the relationship with IHL as lex specialis.

Bantekas and Oette criticise Ilaşcu v Moldova and Russia (2004) for diluting the effective control test 'without sufficient legal justification': Russia had jurisdiction because the Transdniestrian regime stayed 'under the effective authority, or at the very least under the decisive influence' of Russia and survived thanks to its military, economic and political support. Contrast the ICJ's far more rigid 'complete dependence' test for treating a proxy as a State organ (Bosnia v Serbia 2007). Useful for the attribution-versus-jurisdiction debate in Ukraine and the Netherlands v Russia.
lecture: Why it matters (Powderly): post-9/11 practice — detention abroad, strikes overseas, surveillance. Duffy: 'post-9/11 practice highlights the manipulation of the extraterritoriality issue to avoid applicability of human rights law'. The US (Guantánamo, rendition, Iraq, Afghanistan), Israel and the UK resisted. Yet obligations apply abroad 'so far as [a State] exercises a sufficient degree of power, authority or control'.

Treaty wording: ICCPR Art 2(1) 'within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction'; ECHR Art 1 'within their jurisdiction'; ACHR Art 1(1); CRC Art 2(1); CAT Art 2(1) 'any territory under its jurisdiction'. The ICESCR and African Charter have no jurisdiction clause.

Jurisdiction means something different in IHRL: in general IL it allocates competences (Zwanenberg); in IHRL it delimits who is protected — whether the person was within the State's power, not whether that power was lawfully exercised.

Loss of control over one's own territory: the presumption of territorial jurisdiction can be rebutted, but positive obligations remain — reassert sovereignty and secure rights where possible (Ilaşcu v Moldova and Russia). Treaty bodies say obligations continue over the whole territory, at least negative ones (HRC recommendations to Ukraine 2022).
Issa v Turkey: Art 1 cannot allow a State to commit violations abroad that it could not commit at home — the core rationale, repeated in Carter.

Spatial model: Loizidou (1995) — effective control of an area through armed forces or a subordinate local administration, whether the military action was lawful or not. Banković (2001) para 71: extraterritorial jurisdiction is exceptional; the bombing of RTS was not covered.

Personal model, as summarised in Ukraine and the Netherlands v Russia (dec. 2022) paras 570–571, building on Al-Skeini paras 136–137 (para 138 is the spatial model): custody abroad (Öcalan, Al-Skeini), significantly curtailed freedom of movement (Medvedyev v France), isolated and specific acts with an element of proximity (Isaak v Turkey's beating and shooting; Carter's targeted killing). Exercise of public powers with consent (Al-Skeini para 135).

Georgia v Russia (II) (2021): paras 83 and 126 — during the active phase (8–12 August 2008), bombing and shelling in a 'context of chaos' means no effective control over territory and (para 137) no State agent authority over individuals; paras 142–143 — only IHL governs, and it is for States to give the Court such a task. Jurisdiction existed in the occupation phase (para 196: IHL occupation implies effective control, though effective control is broader).

Implications the lecture raises: civilians bombed by their own State in a NIAC (Isayeva, Esmukhambetov v Russia) can reach the Court, but those bombed abroad in an IAC cannot — is the Court retreating from harmonious interplay with IHL? Would an individual application differ from an inter-State one?

Carter v Russia (2021): the power to kill implies control. Paras 128–130 — targeted killings by agents abroad outside a military operation fall within jurisdiction (proximity principle extended beyond borders), consistent with Art 15(2), which only exempts deaths from lawful acts of war. Question: does 'proximity' make sense?

Ukraine and the Netherlands v Russia: MH17 and wider violations in Donbass. Grand Chamber decision on jurisdiction and admissibility adopted 30 November 2022 (delivered 25 January 2023); Grand Chamber judgment 9 July 2025. Key questions: can the missile launch by separatists be attributed to Russia, how attribution relates to Art 1 jurisdiction, and whether the Court would revisit the 'context of chaos'.

cases.name: Banković v Belgium and Others
cases.holding: Victims of the NATO aerial bombing of RTS in Belgrade were not within the jurisdiction of the respondent States. Jurisdiction is primarily territorial; the Convention operates in the 'espace juridique' of Europe and rights can't be divided and tailored.
cases.use: The restrictive baseline (later abandoned in part).

cases.name: Al-Skeini v UK
cases.holding: The UK exercised public powers in south-east Iraq, and through its soldiers' security operations it had authority and control over individuals killed, so Art 2 applied, including the procedural duty to investigate. Rights can be divided and tailored.
cases.use: Spatial and personal models; the duty to investigate abroad.

cases.name: Georgia v Russia (II)
cases.holding: No jurisdiction over the active phase of hostilities (bombing and shelling) because of the 'context of chaos'. Jurisdiction existed over the subsequent occupation, detention, and the duty to investigate.
cases.use: The limits in hostilities; critique (Milanovic).

cases.name: Carter v Russia
cases.holding: The poisoning of Litvinenko in London by Russian agents was within Russia's jurisdiction because the agents exercised physical power and control over his life. Art 2 was violated.
cases.use: The functional-personal model for targeted killing.

cases.name: Ukraine and the Netherlands v Russia (merits)
cases.holding: 9 July 2025, unanimous. Russia responsible for administrative practices of grave violations in eastern Ukraine and in the full-scale invasion (11 May 2014 – 16 Sept 2022). Jurisdiction extends to military attacks during active hostilities (Georgia (II) confined to its facts). MH17: Arts 2, 3, 13 violated. Just satisfaction reserved.
cases.use: Jurisdiction over active hostilities; attribution vs jurisdiction; IHL-informed Art 2.

cases.name: Sacchi et al. v Argentina et al.
cases.holding: The children were within the jurisdiction of the respondent States because of the foreseeable transboundary harm of emissions within the States' effective control (applying OC-23). The communication was inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies.
cases.use: The functional model in climate cases.

cases.name: Lebedeva and Others v Russia (strike-out)
cases.holding: Decision of 7 July 2026 (published 3 Sept 2026) struck out 879 remaining individual applications under Art 37(1)(c), citing Russia's refusal to execute judgments. Russia's international responsibility is unaffected, and about 5,700 conflict-related applications remain.
cases.use: Effectiveness limits after expulsion (Art 58: Russia ceased to be a party 16 Sept 2022).

cards.q: What are the three models of extraterritorial jurisdiction?
cards.a: Spatial (effective control over an area: Loizidou, Al-Skeini para 138); personal (State agent authority and control over a person: Öcalan, Al-Skeini paras 136–137); functional or impact (control over the enjoyment of the right: GC 36 para 63, OC-23, Sacchi).

cards.q: Why is Georgia v Russia II criticised?
cards.a: It denies jurisdiction for the most lethal acts (bombing in active hostilities) while finding it for lesser acts, a return to Banković. It creates a perverse incentive and contrasts with Carter v Russia.

cards.q: What is 'dividing and tailoring' rights?
cards.a: When exercising authority and control over an individual abroad, the State must secure the rights relevant to that situation, not the full catalogue (Al-Skeini para 137, reversing Banković).

cards.q: Jurisdiction (Art 1 ECHR) versus attribution (ARSIWA)?
cards.a: Jurisdiction is a threshold for treaty obligations to arise (control over area or person). Attribution determines whether conduct is the State's. The ECtHR sometimes merges them, e.g. for proxies in Ukraine and Netherlands v Russia.

cards.q: How does 'jurisdiction' in IHRL differ from jurisdiction in general international law?
cards.a: In general IL it allocates State competences to act (prescribe, adjudicate, enforce). In IHRL it delimits the persons protected: whether the individual was within the State's power or control, regardless of whether that power was lawfully established.

cards.q: What did Georgia v Russia (II) decide on the active phase of hostilities?
cards.a: No jurisdiction: in a 'context of chaos' during bombing and shelling there is neither effective control over territory (para 126) nor State agent authority over individuals (para 137); such acts are governed by IHL (paras 142–143). Jurisdiction did exist for the subsequent occupation, detention and the duty to investigate.

cards.q: What is the 'Issa principle'?
cards.a: Art 1 ECHR cannot be interpreted to let a State perpetrate violations on another State's territory that it could not perpetrate on its own (Issa v Turkey; repeated in Carter v Russia para 128).

excerpts.text: …while the jurisdiction of States is primarily territorial, it may sometimes be exercised outside the national territory. Considering the object and purpose of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, it would seem natural that, even when such is the case, States parties to the Covenant should be bound to comply with its provisions.
excerpts.why: The ICCPR applies extraterritorially (Art 2(1) read disjunctively); HRC GC 31 para 10.

excerpts.text: It is clear that, whenever the State, through its agents, exercises control and authority over an individual, and thus jurisdiction, the State is under an obligation under Article 1 to secure to that individual the rights and freedoms under Section I of the Convention that are relevant to the situation of that individual. In this sense, therefore, the Convention rights can be 'divided and tailored'.
excerpts.why: The personal model, which departs from Banković's 'indivisible' rights.

excerpts.text: …the United Kingdom… assumed in Iraq the exercise of some of the public powers normally to be exercised by a sovereign government… In these exceptional circumstances, the Court considers that the United Kingdom, through its soldiers engaged in security operations in Basra… exercised authority and control over individuals killed in the course of such security operations…
excerpts.why: The public powers hook: why the Basra killings fell within UK jurisdiction.
