mindmap.title: Extraterritorial human rights jurisdiction
mindmap.blurb: Eight branches and 40 topics, each with its authorities and key quotes. Includes recall mode and search.

topics.title: Human rights mechanisms
core: Charter-based UN system: the Human Rights Council (47 members), Universal Periodic Review (peer review of all States), Special Procedures (independent rapporteurs and working groups), Commissions of Inquiry and fact-finding missions (Syria, Myanmar, Ukraine, OPT), and the OHCHR (High Commissioner).

Treaty bodies (ten committees, e.g. HRC, CESCR, CAT, CRC, CEDAW, CERD): State reporting with concluding observations, individual communications (optional protocols or declarations), interstate complaints, inquiry procedures, and General Comments (authoritative but non-binding interpretations).
UNESCO: the right to education, culture, science, and freedom of expression (the often-forgotten limb).

European system: the ECtHR has compulsory jurisdiction and binding judgments (Art 46), supervised by the Committee of Ministers, with individual petition (Art 34). Subsidiarity and margin of appreciation (Protocol 15). Russia was expelled from the CoE in March 2022.

Inter-American system: the Commission (petitions, precautionary measures, country reports) filters cases to the Court. Broad reparations (restitution, rehabilitation, satisfaction, guarantees of non-repetition), conventionality control, and progressive advisory opinions (OC-23 environment, OC-32/25 climate emergency).

African system: the African Commission and the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights. Individuals and NGOs can access the Court only if the State has made an Art 34(6) declaration (several withdrawals: Rwanda, Tanzania, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire). The Charter has peoples' rights and duties.

Admissibility typology (Scheinin): victim status (direct, indirect, potential victims; no actio popularis before the ECtHR or HRC); exhaustion of effective domestic remedies; time limits (ECtHR four months since Protocol 15); not the same matter before another international body; ratione personae, materiae, loci, temporis; significant disadvantage (ECHR Art 35(3)(b)).
Third-party intervention (Art 36 ECHR): States and NGOs as amici, increasingly strategic.

Strategic litigation (Duffy's inaugural lecture): litigation is valuable beyond winning (agenda setting, empowerment, norm development), but the 'champagne moment' of a judgment rarely ends the struggle. Compliance and implementation are where impact happens.

Pushback and backlash: withdrawals (US from the HRC; Art 34(6) withdrawals), non-compliance (Russia, Turkey: Kavala, an Art 46(4) infringement), the Copenhagen and Brighton declarations, and the politicisation of mechanisms.

UN fact-finding before the ICJ: in Gambia v Myanmar (2026) the Court, with no ICTY-style judgments available, built its factual findings mainly on the HRC Fact-Finding Mission reports (rigorous methodology, comparable to or exceeding earlier UN reports, para 112) and the IIMM's analytical reports and witness statements ('considerable evidential weight', para 119). It disregarded their legal conclusions (para 100) and drew more liberal inferences because Myanmar refused access (paras 128-131).

Duffy, a 'skeptical believer' in litigation, proposes three lenses for judging strategic litigation: a high-definition lens (impact on several dimensions: victims and survivors, the law, political and social change, democracy and the rule of law), a long lens (impact before, during and long after judgment), and a wide-angle lens (litigation working alongside advocacy, education and law reform). Impact can be negative too: unimplemented wins, backlash, 'bad cases make bad law'. Guantánamo shows the ambivalence: Lobel calls Boumediene a 'pyrrhic victory', Duffy stresses its expressive value. Her image: a kaleidoscope, not a camera, and 'smaller champagne moments'.

African Court access (Plagis): the Art 34(6) declaration has been called the 'price' of creating the Court and is its biggest barrier; only ten States ever made one, and four withdrew (Rwanda, Tanzania, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire). In Umuhoza v Rwanda (2016) the Court held the declaration is separable from the Protocol and may be withdrawn, but only with one year's notice for legal certainty (following IACtHR Ivcher Bronstein v Peru), so pending and new cases filed in that year remain admissible. In Falana v AU dissenting judges found Art 34(6) inconsistent with the Charter, but the Court cannot set it aside.

The African Court's material jurisdiction is the broadest of the regional courts: Art 3(1) of the Protocol covers the Charter and 'any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the States concerned' (e.g. the ECOWAS Democracy Protocol in APDH v Côte d'Ivoire, 2016). The UDHR may be used as custom only where the right is also in a ratified treaty (Omary v Tanzania, 2014). Applicants need not cite Charter articles (Chacha v Tanzania). The Court reviews national proceedings for manifest arbitrariness but is not an appeal court and does not apply domestic law (Abubakari v Tanzania).
lecture: Lecture 8 opened on the 80th anniversary of the Nuremberg judgment (1 October 1946).

Human Rights Council: a subsidiary organ of the GA. Tools: UPR; Special Procedures; the confidential complaint procedure (formerly '1503') for patterns of gross violations, not individual cases; Commissions of Inquiry; an Advisory Committee of 18 experts.

UPR: every UN member reviewed every four and a half years, 42 States a year, by a troika, on three documents (national report, UN compilation, stakeholders' summary). States 'accept' or 'note' recommendations; over 56,000 made in the first two cycles; roughly half reportedly lead to action. Non-confrontational peer review.

Special Procedures (GA Res 60/251): independent unpaid experts, 46 thematic and 14 country mandates; communications (letters of allegation, urgent appeals), country visits, standing invitations, annual reports, collective statements.

Treaty bodies: State reporting (with a review procedure for chronic non-reporters); inquiries by CAT, CEDAW, CESCR, CRPD and CRC into grave or systematic violations if the State accepted competence; CED has extra powers (urgent action to search for a disappeared person, referral of widespread or systematic disappearances to the GA). Inter-State complaints are possible under several treaties. The slides say none has been brought, but three were lodged under CERD Art 11 in 2018 (Qatar v Saudi Arabia, Qatar v UAE, State of Palestine v Israel), the first inter-State communications before a treaty body. Individual complaints exist for all except the CMW: written, confidential, no legal aid.
OHCHR: called for at the 1993 Vienna World Conference, created by GA Res 48/141; the High Commissioner is appointed by the SG and approved by the GA for a renewable four-year term.

ECtHR: individual petition was optional until Protocol 11 (1998) abolished the Commission and made the Court central; Protocol 16 (2013) allows advisory opinions. Priority categories I–VII (urgent cases first, core rights Arts 2, 3, 4, 5(1) in category III, manifestly inadmissible last). Interim measures are binding.

Inter-American system: the American Declaration (1948) and ACHR (1969: 22 of 35 OAS States, not the US or Canada). The Commission (7 members) handles every petition first, seeks friendly settlement, issues precautionary measures and country reports. The Court (1979, 7 part-time judges; 20 States accept its contentious jurisdiction): only the Commission and States can refer cases; very influential reparations and advisory opinions.

African system: the Banjul Charter (1981) includes collective rights and duties. The Commission (11 members, since 1987) accepts communications from NGOs and non-victims, applies exhaustion flexibly, and has biennial State reporting and its own special rapporteurs. The Court (Protocol 1998, in force 2004, Arusha, 11 judges) hears individuals and NGOs only where an Art 34(6) declaration exists (only 8 States). The ECOWAS Court does not require exhaustion. Nascent: ASEAN (2012 Declaration and Commission), the Arab and Gulf systems.

Treaty-body admissibility (Lecture 9): direct victim, no actio popularis; ratione temporis, including continuing effects; not the same matter before another international body (the ICCPR and CED only bar simultaneous examination, allowing forum shopping, but many ECHR States have reservations); exhaustion unless unreasonably prolonged. 'Views' are not binding; follow-up rapporteurs; GA Res 68/268 (2014) on harmonising working methods. Debate: should views be binding, and are they effective remedies?

Victim status under ECHR Art 34: person, NGO or group of individuals directly affected or at genuine risk; not 'rigid, mechanical and inflexible' (Gorraiz Lizarraga v Spain); read in light of present-day conditions (Loizidou).

KlimaSeniorinnen (9 April 2024): building on López Ostra and Öneryıldız on environmental positive obligations, and domestic precedents (Urgenda, the German Klimabeschluss). Art 8 covers climate mitigation; Switzerland failed to do what it could (para 451 on subsidiarity). For individuals, a 'special approach' to victim status — high-intensity exposure and a pressing need for individual protection — set so high that none qualified; associations can have standing if lawfully established, dedicated to defending members' rights, and genuinely representative. The lecture's critique: individuals suffer harm, not legal entities; the reasoning leans on 'common concern of humankind'. The judgment is declaratory, leaving measures to Switzerland and the Committee of Ministers.

cases.name: Kavala v Turkey (Art 46(4))
cases.holding: Turkey failed to comply with the 2019 judgment ordering Kavala's release. This was the second-ever infringement procedure.
cases.use: The compliance gap; backlash.

cases.name: Billy et al. v Australia (Torres Strait Islanders)
cases.holding: Australia's failure to adapt to climate impacts violated Art 17 (home and family life) and Art 27 (minority culture). Art 6 (life) was not yet violated given the timeframe.
cases.use: Treaty-body communications; climate as a human rights issue.

cards.q: What are the main admissibility criteria before the ECtHR?
cards.a: Victim status (Art 34); exhaustion of domestic remedies; the four-month time limit; not substantially the same as a matter already examined; not manifestly ill-founded; significant disadvantage; compatibility ratione personae, materiae, loci and temporis (Art 35).

cards.q: Charter-based versus treaty-based UN mechanisms?
cards.a: Charter-based: they derive from the UN Charter and apply to all members (HRC, UPR, Special Procedures, COIs). Treaty-based: they derive from specific treaties and bind only parties (committees: reporting, communications, General Comments).

cards.q: How does access to the African Court work?
cards.a: States, the Commission and African IGOs can submit cases. Individuals and NGOs only where the State made an Art 34(6) Protocol declaration, and several States have withdrawn theirs.

cards.q: What is Duffy's 'champagne moment'?
cards.a: The celebration of a litigation victory. Her point is that judgments rarely end the matter: strategic litigation's impact lies in broader processes of mobilisation, implementation and norm change, so judge it beyond the courtroom.

cards.q: UPR in numbers?
cards.a: Every UN member every 4.5 years; 42 States a year in three two-week sessions; a troika of States; three base documents; recommendations accepted or noted; 56,000+ in the first two cycles; around half reportedly lead to action.

cards.q: Who can bring a case to the Inter-American Court, and to the African Court?
cards.a: Inter-American: only the Commission and States parties (individuals must go through the Commission). African: States, the African Commission and African IGOs; individuals and NGOs only against States that made an Art 34(6) declaration (only 8).

cards.q: What were the victim-status criteria in KlimaSeniorinnen?
cards.a: Individuals: high-intensity exposure to the adverse effects of climate change and a pressing need for individual protection (not met). Associations: lawfully established, dedicated statutory purpose of defending members' human rights against climate threats, and genuinely qualified and representative (met).

cards.q: What are Duffy's three lenses and four dimensions of litigation impact?
cards.a: Lenses: high-definition (detailed, multi-dimensional impact), long (before, during and long after judgment), wide-angle (litigation in context with advocacy and reform). Dimensions: victims and survivors, the law, political and social change, democracy and the rule of law. Impact can be negative (backlash, unimplemented wins). Hence 'smaller champagne moments' rather than one judgment day.

cards.q: Can a State withdraw its Art 34(6) declaration, and with what effect (Umuhoza v Rwanda)?
cards.a: Yes: the declaration is separable from the Protocol and withdrawable at the State's discretion, but not with immediate effect. For legal certainty a one-year notice period applies (drawing on Ivcher Bronstein v Peru), during which applications can still be filed; the Court applied the same period to Tanzania (Cheusi v Tanzania 2020). Compare Rome Statute Art 127 (one year) and GC 26 on the ICCPR (no withdrawal).

topics.title: International criminal justice: history and the ICC
core: IMT Nuremberg (London Charter 1945, Art 6): crimes against peace, war crimes, and CAH (linked to war). Individual responsibility, no defence of superior orders (mitigation only), and official position no bar. 2026 is the 80th anniversary of the judgment.

The IMTFE (Tokyo), Control Council Law No. 10 (zonal trials; CAH not linked to war), and the UN War Crimes Commission (an early form of complementarity, supporting national trials). Asia trials (Sellars). The 'victor's justice' critique (tu quoque, selectivity, ex post facto).

Legacies: the Nuremberg Principles (ILC 1950), the Genocide Convention (1948), the Geneva Conventions (1949, the Grave Breaches regime), and the ILC draft code. The Cold War froze plans for a permanent court.

The ICTY (1993) and ICTR (1994) were created by SC resolutions under Chapter VII (Tadić upheld their legality), with primacy over national courts. Innovations: NIAC war crimes, CAH without a war nexus, rape as genocide and torture (Akayesu, Furundžija), JCE, and command responsibility.
Hybrid tribunals: SCSL (Taylor), ECCC, STL (terrorism), and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Rome Statute (1998, in force 2002): the debates were OTP independence (proprio motu with PTC review, Art 15), the SC role (referral under Art 13(b) and deferral under Art 16), complementarity (Art 17), immunities (Art 27 versus Art 98), aggression (deferred to Kampala), and victims (participation under Art 68(3), reparations under Art 75, the Trust Fund).

ICC jurisdiction: subject matter (Art 5), temporal (after 1 July 2002, Art 11), preconditions (territory or nationality of a State party or an Art 12(3) declarant, Art 12), triggers (State referral, SC referral, proprio motu under Art 13).

Admissibility (Art 17): a case is inadmissible if genuinely investigated or prosecuted by a State with jurisdiction, unless that State is unwilling (shielding, undue delay, lack of independence) or unable (collapse of the judicial system). The test is the same person and substantially the same conduct (Ruto, Gaddafi, Al-Senussi). Gravity applies under Art 17(1)(d). The two-step approach: is there an investigation, and is it genuine?

Immunities: Art 27 (official capacity irrelevant) versus Art 98(1). Al-Bashir Jordan Appeal (2019): there is no customary Head-of-State immunity before international courts, and an SC referral binds Sudan as if a party. Art 87(7) non-compliance findings: Mongolia (Putin, 2024), Hungary (Netanyahu, PTC I 24 July 2025), Italy (Almasri, 17 Oct 2025; referred 2026), Tajikistan (Putin's Oct 2025 visit; referred to the ASP 7 May 2026: a CIS immunity agreement cannot override Rome obligations).

Withdrawal (Art 127): it takes effect one year after notification, and the Court keeps jurisdiction over crimes committed while the State was a party. Burundi (authorised before its withdrawal took effect, Oct 2017). Philippines (withdrawal effective 17 Mar 2019; investigation only authorised 15 Sept 2021): Duterte Appeals Judgment of 22 Apr 2026 holds that a preliminary examination opened before withdrawal is a 'matter already under consideration by the Court' (Art 127(2)). Duterte: surrendered 12 Mar 2025; 3 CAH counts (murder and attempted murder) confirmed 23 Apr 2026; found fit (28 Sept 2026); trial opens 30 Nov 2026.

Contemporary challenges: US sanctions under EO 14203 (Feb 2025) on the Prosecutor, both deputies, 9 of 18 judges incl. President Akane (Aug 2026), and the ICC itself as an entity (9 Oct 2026); withdrawals by Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali (June 2026), Venezuela and Chad (July 2026), while Hungary revoked its withdrawal (29 May 2026); Prosecutor Khan removed by the ASP (24 July 2026); resources; the neo-imperial critique; Israel's challenges (Art 18 rejected by Appeals 15 Dec 2025; Art 19(2) jurisdiction challenge on remand pending).

Turning away from the ICC? The Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine (CoE–Ukraine agreement 25 June 2025; Rada ratification 15 July 2025; Enlarged Partial Agreement CM/Res(2026)5, 15 May 2026; seat in The Hague, full operations expected 2027), and domestic universal and extraterritorial jurisdiction (91 cases in 20 States in 2025, UJAR 2026): Koblenz al-Khatib on Syria; Lafarge convicted in Paris of financing terrorism in Syria (13 Apr 2026; CAH-complicity investigation continues); the Lundin Sudan war-crimes trial in Stockholm (verdict expected Dec 2026). 'Is the future domestic?'

Convergence of ICJ and ICL on genocide: Gambia v Myanmar (2026) treats 'only reasonable inference' as a general ICL test (Tolimir; Stakic) (para 442), reads superior responsibility into Art IV of the Genocide Convention (para 522), and relies on IIMM evidence collected to criminal standards (para 119). State and individual responsibility nonetheless remain distinct regimes, and State responsibility is 'not of a criminal nature' (para 295).

Fitness to stand trial at the ICC (Duterte, Trial Chamber III, decision of 28 Sept 2026, public 8 Oct 2026): fitness is 'an aspect of the broader notion of fair trial' (Arts 63(1), 64(8)(a), 67; Art 21(3) imports human rights). The test is whether the accused can meaningfully exercise his procedural rights: understand the conduct, purpose and possible consequences of the proceedings, instruct counsel and, if he wishes, make a statement, 'viewed overall and in a reasonable manner'. A medical diagnosis, or loss of memory of the events, is not decisive in itself. If unfit, the trial is adjourned (Rule 135(4)), not terminated. The Chamber relied on a unanimous three-expert panel, refused further tests and refused to let the Defence question the experts, ordered accommodations (hearing support, care with food and rest, a nurse) and continuous monitoring. Pre-Trial Chamber I had already found him fit for the pre-trial stage on 26 Jan 2026.

Unfitness precedents: Kabuga (IRMCT) was found unfit with dementia in June 2023 and died on 16 May 2026 with his trial unfinished; Ieng Thirith (ECCC) was found unfit in 2011, proceedings were stayed in 2012 and she died in 2015; Pinochet was declared unfit by Chile's Supreme Court in 2002 (though later rulings varied). Lesson: if fitness fails, ICL produces no verdict at all, and a fitness ruling is a snapshot, while a trial is a film. Empirical caution: one Australian study found opposing experts disagreed on fitness in 33 of 108 report pairs (Large et al 2009).

Chiarini on Duterte and Art 127: the Appeals Chamber majority (22 Apr 2026) turned the preliminary examination, an internal and unregulated prosecutorial step that can begin with reading an NGO report, into a mechanism that preserves jurisdiction beyond the one-year window, making withdrawal 'largely symbolic'. He prefers the dissents (de Brichambaut and Lordkipanidze 2023; Lordkipanidze 2026): the Art 12 preconditions must exist when jurisdiction is triggered, which under Art 13(c) means PTC authorisation, and 'one year is sufficient'. Whiting's point: it is incongruous that the Court keeps jurisdiction over a preliminary examination while the departing State's duty to cooperate covers only 'investigations and proceedings' begun before withdrawal (Art 127(2)). Use: legality and foreseeability versus the anti-impunity purpose.

Clapham's criminalisation point feeds the selectivity debate: through self-referrals (Uganda, CAR, DRC, Mali, Gabon) governments cooperate with the ICC so that non-state actors are tried, so the first ICC trials 'veered towards' rebel leaders rather than State agents, while prosecutions of State officials meet immunities and other obstacles (and the Malabo Protocol, Art 46A bis, protects serving leaders). Read with Bikundo's 'selective universality': one segment of humanity judging another.

Meron's defence of international criminal justice: the fact that atrocities continue does not disprove deterrence, any more than continuing murders disprove domestic criminal law. Tribunals also serve other goals: exposing the leaders who fanned hatred, education, supporting refugee return, building procedural law, and training a generation of lawyers. But ICL 'does not provide all the answers': national courts bear primary responsibility, combined with asset freezes, travel bans and stigmatisation. Jackson at Nuremberg: 'one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason'.

Complementarity debates for essays: inaction makes a case admissible without asking whether the State is unwilling or unable (Katanga, Appeals Chamber, 25 Sept 2009), which Robinson defends as simpler than critics claim ('The Mysterious Mysteriousness of Complementarity', 2010). Heller's 'shadow side': Art 17 does not let the ICC find a State 'unwilling' because its proceedings are unfair to the accused, so it pressures States towards harsh processes and convictions. On universal jurisdiction as the alternative, Langer shows it gravitates towards 'low-cost defendants' whose States will not retaliate ('The Diplomacy of Universal Jurisdiction' (2011) 105 AJIL 1).
lecture: What is ICL (Heinsch): international rules creating direct individual responsibility for 'the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole' — the four core crimes. Open question on the slides: should drug trafficking, human trafficking and slavery, terrorism, corruption or torture also count?

Two problems for ICL within PIL: individuals long lacked rights and duties (exceptions: piracy, war crimes, cable crimes), and enforcement is horizontal (no real executive, no compulsory jurisdiction). ICL's 'double nature': criminal law (repression, detail, rights of the accused) and PIL (diplomacy, prevention, ambiguity) — a hybrid and a patchwork of common- and civil-law principles; its rules come from PIL sources and are interpreted by PIL rules.

Early precedents: Conradin of Hohenstaufen (1268, 'unjust war'); Peter von Hagenbach (1474, siege of Breisach). Versailles 1919 Art 227: Kaiser Wilhelm II indicted but the Netherlands refused extradition. The interwar League convention for an ICC never entered into force.

1945 IMT (London Agreement, Art 6(a)–(c)); 1946 IMTFE; 1948 Genocide Convention; 1949 Geneva Conventions with grave breaches; 1950 ILC Nuremberg Principles; 1953 draft ICC statute; 1954 draft Code of Offences; halted in 1957 by the Cold War.

Breakthrough: ILC resumes 1989; ICTY 1993 and ICTR 1994 (Chapter VII, IHL violations as a threat to peace); Tadić jurisdiction decision 1995; ILC Draft Code 1996; Rome Statute 1998, in force 2002. ICTY (closed 31 Dec 2017): grave breaches, laws or customs of war, genocide, CAH, no head-of-State immunity. ICTR (closed 31 Dec 2015): genocide, CAH, CA3 and APII violations — the first recognition of individual responsibility in NIAC. The IRMCT took over.

Mixed tribunals: Kosovo (1999), East Timor (2000), SCSL (2002, Charles Taylor), Bosnia War Crimes Chamber (2002), ECCC (2003), Iraqi High Tribunal (2003/4), STL (2007), Kosovo Specialist Chambers (2015), Special Criminal Court CAR (2015), Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine (2025).

Complementarity two-step (Art 17): (i) is there a national investigation or prosecution of the case? (ii) if so, is the State unwilling (shielding, unjustified delay, lack of independence — Art 17(2)) or unable (total or substantial collapse or unavailability of the judicial system — Art 17(3))? Same case: same person and substantially the same conduct (Ruto, Muthaura 2011); Gaddafi and Al-Senussi (PTC 2013): not the same incidents but the same gravamen of the crime.

Gravity (Arts 17(1)(d), 53(1)(c)): scale, nature, manner of commission, impact (Comoros flotilla situation). Interests of justice (Art 53(1)(c), (2)(c)): deference to transitional justice and amnesties is the problem — e.g. Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace.

ICC procedure (Lecture 11): a hybrid of adversarial (contest between parties, disclosure, guilty plea) and inquisitorial (prosecutor gathers a dossier, judge-led trial, victim participation) models; early tribunals were adversarial, the ICC integrates civil-law features. 18 judges (List A criminal law, List B international law, six elected every three years); Pre-Trial, Trial and Appeals Divisions (PTC authorises proprio motu investigations, rules on jurisdiction and admissibility, issues warrants, confirms charges — Arts 15, 19, 57, 58, 61). Prosecutor elected for 9 years; 'situations, not cases' (18 situations, 34 cases). Rights of the accused (Arts 63, 66–67); victims participate (Art 68(3)) and claim reparations (Art 75).

Immunities saga: Art 27 versus Art 98(1). Al-Bashir/Jordan (Appeals 2019): no customary head-of-State immunity before an international court, including for States executing its requests. Putin/Mongolia (PTC 2024): applied without an SC referral; Mongolia breached cooperation duties. Netanyahu/Hungary (PTC 2025): non-compliance, referral to the ASP under Art 87(7). Critics contest the customary basis for non-parties; the Court depends on States to enforce.

Existential pressures (2025–26): US Executive Order 14203 (2025) targeting ICC work; on 9 Oct 2026 the ICC condemned sanctions against the institution itself. Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali notified withdrawal in June 2026 (effective June 2027); Hungary rescinded its notice on 29 May 2026. On 24 July 2026 the ASP removed Prosecutor Karim Khan under Art 46 for serious misconduct. Budget and liquidity constraints force prioritisation.

Neo-imperial critique: unequal exposure, early African focus, whose account of violence counts, selective political support. Complicating it: self-referrals by Uganda, the DRC, CAR and Mali; the Ukraine and Palestine situations; independence within an unequal order. Question posed: would abandoning the ICC reduce unequal justice or remove an avenue for victims?

Turning away from the ICC? Universal jurisdiction: Belgium and Spain narrowed their 'absolute' laws after diplomatic fallout; Germany gives the prosecutor discretion without a territorial link. The Ukraine aggression tribunal (CoE–Ukraine Agreement, 25 June 2025) fills the Art 15 bis(5) gap; serving troika members keep personal immunity; funding, enforcement and selectivity remain challenges.

cases.name: IMT Nuremberg judgment
cases.holding: Aggressive war is 'the supreme international crime'. Crimes against IL are committed by men, not abstract entities. Individuals have duties transcending national obedience.
cases.use: The foundations of individual responsibility.

cases.name: Al-Bashir (Jordan Referral Appeal)
cases.holding: There is no customary Head-of-State immunity vis-à-vis an international court. Art 27 applies to Sudan via SC Res 1593, and Jordan breached its duty to arrest.
cases.use: Immunities and cooperation.

cases.name: Situation in the Philippines / Prosecutor v Duterte (jurisdiction)
cases.court: ICC PTC I; Appeals Chamber (22 Apr 2026)
cases.holding: Investigation authorised (2021) and resumption upheld (Appeals 2023) despite withdrawal effective 17 Mar 2019. In Duterte the Appeals Chamber (majority, Lordkipanidze partly dissenting) held that Art 12(2) must be read with Art 127, and that the pre-withdrawal preliminary examination (opened and announced Feb 2018) was a 'matter under consideration by the Court' (Art 127(2)), 'the Court' there including the OTP. Burundi was distinguished, since there the investigation was authorised before withdrawal took effect. Charges confirmed 23 Apr 2026; trial from 30 Nov 2026.
cases.use: Art 127 withdrawal; complementarity.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Gaddafi and Al-Senussi (admissibility)
cases.holding: Gaddafi's case was admissible (Libya unable to secure custody or evidence). Al-Senussi's was inadmissible (genuine domestic proceedings).
cases.use: The 'same person, same conduct' test; unable versus unwilling.

cases.name: Kony (confirmation in absentia)
cases.holding: On 6 Nov 2025 all 39 counts of war crimes and CAH were confirmed in Kony's absence: the first in absentia confirmation (Art 61(2)(b)); the Appeals Chamber upheld the framework on 3 June 2025. Trial cannot proceed without the accused (Art 63).
cases.use: Fugitive suspects; limits of the ICC; contrast with the Special Tribunal's Art 28 in absentia trials.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Katanga and Ngudjolo (admissibility appeal)
cases.holding: Where no State with jurisdiction is investigating or prosecuting, the case is admissible; the unwillingness and inability questions in Art 17(2)–(3) arise only once there is national activity concerning the case ('inaction' makes a case admissible).
cases.use: Step one of the Art 17 test; self-referrals (the DRC surrendered him rather than prosecuting him for these crimes).

cards.q: What are the three ICC trigger mechanisms, and when do the Art 12 preconditions apply?
cards.a: State party referral (Art 14), SC referral under Chapter VII (13(b), no Art 12 preconditions), and the Prosecutor proprio motu with PTC authorisation (Art 15). Art 12 (territory or nationality of a State party or declarant) applies to State referral and proprio motu.

cards.q: What is the Art 17 admissibility test?
cards.a: Inadmissible if the case is being, or has been, genuinely investigated or prosecuted, unless the State is unwilling or unable; also ne bis in idem and insufficient gravity. Step 1: is there an actual investigation of the same person for substantially the same conduct? Step 2: is it genuine?

cards.q: What happens to ICC jurisdiction when a State withdraws?
cards.a: Withdrawal takes effect one year after notification (Art 127). The Court retains jurisdiction over crimes committed while the State was a party, and the State's duty to cooperate covers matters already under consideration before the effective date (Art 127(2)). Burundi: investigation authorised before the withdrawal took effect. Philippines: authorised only in 2021, after the 2019 withdrawal, but the Appeals Chamber (Duterte, 22 Apr 2026) held that the preliminary examination opened in Feb 2018 was already a 'matter under consideration'.

cards.q: Name three Rome conference fault lines.
cards.a: OTP independence (proprio motu); the SC's role (referral and Art 16 deferral); complementarity; immunities and cooperation; the definition of aggression; victim participation.

cards.q: What is the victor's justice critique of Nuremberg?
cards.a: Only Axis defendants were tried; Allied crimes (Dresden, Katyn) were excluded; crimes against peace arguably ex post facto; judges came from the victor States. Also tu quoque arguments.

cards.q: What is 'the same case' for Art 17 admissibility?
cards.a: The same person and substantially the same conduct (Ruto and Muthaura, Appeals 2011). Gaddafi and Al-Senussi (PTC 2013): national proceedings need not cover the same incidents, but must cover the same gravamen or essence of the crime.

cards.q: Name three 2025–26 'existential pressures' on the ICC.
cards.a: US sanctions (EO 14203, 2025; sanctions against the institution itself condemned on 9 Oct 2026); withdrawal notices by Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali (June 2026, effective June 2027), with Hungary rescinding on 29 May 2026; the ASP's removal of Prosecutor Karim Khan under Art 46 (24 July 2026); resource scarcity.

cards.q: How does the ICC's procedure mix legal traditions?
cards.a: Adversarial: party-led evidence, disclosure, cross-examination, guilty pleas (Art 65). Inquisitorial: the Prosecutor must investigate incriminating and exonerating circumstances equally (Art 54(1)(a)), the PTC confirms charges, judges may request evidence (Art 69(3)), victims participate (Art 68(3)), and a single verdict on guilt and sentence is the civil-law model (the slides); at the ICC itself sentencing is normally a separate decision after conviction (Art 76; e.g. Lubanga, Bemba, Ntaganda, Ongwen). Tension: e.g. victim participation versus fair-trial rights and expeditiousness.

cards.q: How was Karim Khan removed, and who runs the OTP?
cards.a: Art 46(2)(b): by an absolute majority of States Parties by secret ballot. At a special ASP session (NY, 24 July 2026), 82 of 125 found serious misconduct and serious breach of duty after an OIOS inquiry; the Bureau had suspended him on 8 June 2026, even though a judges' panel (Mar 2026) reportedly found misconduct not established. Deputy Prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang lead the OTP; applications for a new Prosecutor run 31 Oct 2026 to 31 Jan 2027.

cards.q: Can a State revoke an Art 127 withdrawal before it takes effect, and which withdrawals are pending?
cards.a: Yes: a notification may be revoked before it takes effect (VCLT Art 68): Hungary (notified 2 June 2025, revoked 29 May 2026). Pending: Niger (18 June 2026), Burkina Faso and Mali (June 2026), Venezuela (24 July 2026), Chad (27 July 2026), each effective one year later. Obligations arising while a party continue (Art 127(2)).

cards.q: What did the US do to the ICC on 9 Oct 2026?
cards.a: OFAC listed the ICC itself as an SDN under EO 14203, blocking its US property and barring US persons from providing funds, goods or services, with general licences for wind-down (to 7 Apr 2027), IT, pensions and detention. This came after 13 individual designations (Khan, both deputies, 9 judges incl. President Akane, a trial lawyer). The ICC 'strongly rejected' it the same day.

cards.q: What is the ICC test for fitness to stand trial (Duterte 2026)?
cards.a: Fitness is part of the fair-trial guarantee. The accused must be able to meaningfully exercise his rights: understand the conduct, purpose and consequences of the proceedings, instruct counsel and, if he wishes, make a statement, 'viewed overall and in a reasonable manner'. Memory of the events and diagnoses are not decisive by themselves. Unfit means adjournment (Rule 135(4)). Duterte was found fit on 28 Sept 2026 with accommodations and monitoring.

cards.q: Why do Chiarini and the dissents object to the Duterte jurisdiction ruling?
cards.a: A preliminary examination is an informal, internal OTP process, not an exercise of the Court's jurisdiction. The Art 12 preconditions should exist when jurisdiction is triggered (PTC authorisation under Art 15(4)); the Philippines' withdrawal took effect in March 2019 and authorisation came in Sept 2021. Treating the examination as a 'matter under consideration' lets the Prosecutor freeze jurisdiction indefinitely and makes the one-year window in Art 127 largely symbolic.

mindmap.title: International criminal justice and the ICC
mindmap.blurb: Eight branches and 48 topics, each with its authorities and key quotes. Includes recall mode and search.

topics.title: IHL enforcement and accountability
core: CA1: 'respect and ensure respect in all circumstances'. Internal (train, instruct, discipline, prosecute) and external (do not aid or assist violations; exert influence to bring violations to an end; ICRC 2016 Commentary). It is an obligation of due diligence; the external dimension is debated (US position: not legally binding).

Arms transfers: CA1, the ATT (Art 6: prohibition if knowledge that the arms would be used for genocide, CAH or grave breaches; Art 7: export assessment of the overriding risk of serious IHL violations), and the EU Common Position. Domestic cases: R (CAAT) v Secretary of State (UK Saudi exports, 2019 Court of Appeal: unlawful failure to assess past violations); Dutch Supreme Court on F-35 parts to Israel (3 Oct 2025: it quashed the appeal court's ban because courts may not substitute their own 'clear risk' assessment, and ordered the Minister to reassess under ATT criteria within six weeks; exports stayed halted).

Nicaragua v Germany (ICJ, 2024): Nicaragua alleged breaches of the Genocide Convention and CA1 through arms supply to Israel. Provisional measures were refused (circumstances not requiring them), but the Court reminded all States of their obligations regarding arms transfers.
Military manuals, legal advisers (API Art 82) and military justice systems are where compliance mostly happens. Weapons review (API Art 36).

Grave breaches regime (GCI 49–50; GCII 50–51; GCIII 129–130; GCIV 146–147; API 85): an obligation to search for and prosecute or extradite (aut dedere aut judicare), with mandatory universal jurisdiction. It applies only in IAC.

Command responsibility (API Arts 86–87; Rome Art 28): the superior knew or should have known (military) or consciously disregarded information (civilian), had effective control, and failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent, repress or submit for prosecution. Bemba Appeals (2018) acquitted, emphasising remote commanders' limited measures.

Monitoring: the ICRC (confidential dialogue; the customary IHL study of 2005 with 161 rules), the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (API Art 90, activated for the first time in 2017, at the OSCE's request, to investigate the April 2017 incident in which an OSCE Special Monitoring Mission patrol was hit in eastern Ukraine (Luhansk)), UN COIs mandated by the HRC or SC, and documentation by NGOs.

The failure of the ICRC–Swiss initiative (Pejic 2016): States rejected a meeting of States and periodic reporting at the 2015 International Conference. IHL lacks an institutional compliance mechanism, unlike IHRL.

Accountability through ICL (war crimes) and State responsibility (ICJ; the Art 91 API compensation duty). The NIAC challenge: no grave breaches regime, no combatant immunity, armed groups' capacity, and a lack of reciprocity.

ICC enforcement record 2025–26: El Hishri (Libya, Mitiga prison) surrendered by Germany 1 Dec 2025 with charges confirmed 16 July 2026, whereas Italy released Almasri to Libya (Jan 2025) and was found non-compliant (17 Oct 2025, referred 2026). Cooperation depends on States.

Nicaragua v Germany (Genocide Convention / CA1 arms supply to Israel): provisional measures refused 30 Apr 2024. Nicaragua filed its Memorial 21 July 2025; Germany raised preliminary objections (no prior dispute, jurisdiction, admissibility), heard 7–10 Sept 2026. Judgment pending (likely 2027).

Pejic explains why the ICRC–Swiss process (2012–15) produced so little. While IHL's norms have been updated since 1864, compliance mechanisms 'unique to IHL' remain 'perplexingly absent'. States would not even reconfigure the three existing treaty mechanisms (Protecting Powers, the enquiry procedure, the IHFFC), and insisted that any new Meeting of States be State-driven, consensus-based, voluntary, non-binding, non-politicised, non-contextual and non-selective. Resolution 2 of the 32nd International Conference (2015) merely continued an intergovernmental process. (That process later ended without agreement before the 33rd Conference in 2019.)

Mettraux presents war crimes as IHL's answer to its own enforcement failure: ransom, reparations, reprisals and hostage-taking were all tried and proved ineffective, so individual criminal responsibility was attached to the core prohibitions. This broke two taboos: individuals are bound directly by international (penal) law, and States do not have exclusive jurisdiction, since every belligerent may try war criminals under custom and the idea of an international court grew from Moynier to the Kaiser's planned trial and Nuremberg.
lecture: Implementation in the broad sense (all measures ensuring respect) versus the strict sense (transforming IHL into domestic law). Needs: criminal and disciplinary sanctions; status of persons (combatants, medical and civil defence personnel) and objects; military manuals.

Implementation activities: translation, dissemination, prosecution, marking protected persons and objects, preventing misuse of emblems, training qualified personnel, National Societies, National Information Bureaux. Preventive (dissemination, training, legal advisers) versus repressive (prosecution, disciplinary sanctions).
Enforcement tools listed in sequence: reciprocity; reprisals; public opinion; Chapter VII; Protecting Powers and the ICRC; the Fact-Finding Commission; State and individual responsibility.

Reprisals are limited by subsidiarity (last resort after protest, intermediaries, the SC), proportionality, and the prohibition of force. Treaty prohibitions: wounded and sick (GCI 46, GCII 47), POWs (GCIII 13(3)), protected civilians (GCIV 33(3)), the civilian population (API 51(6)), cultural property (API 53), objects indispensable to survival (API 54(4)), the environment (API 55(2)), dams and nuclear stations (API 56(4)). ICRC customary rules 145–148: stringent conditions in IAC; none against GC-protected persons or objects; no belligerent reprisals in NIAC.

Protecting Power (API Art 2(c)): a neutral State designated by one party and accepted by the other. Tasks: visits, supervision of relief and evacuations, support in legal proceedings, transfer of information, good offices. Used rarely since 1945 (Suez, Goa 1961, India–Pakistan 1971, Falklands 1982).

The ICRC acts in its own name as an impartial, neutral, independent intermediary, not on a party's instructions; parties must allow visits to detainees; it has a right of initiative (Statutes Art 5(3)), especially in NIAC.

International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (API Art 90): permanent, impartial, non-political; competence only for States that accept it in advance or ad hoc; no right of initiative; only States may request; facts only, no legal assessment. First used in Eastern Ukraine at the OSCE's request.
State versus individual responsibility: subject (State versus person), violation (IHL), consequence (reparation versus punishment). Grave breaches of GCs and API are war crimes.

Conclusion on the slides: enforcement has long been problematic; some tools are soft and others (reprisals) may trigger more violations; it became serious only in the last 20 years with ICL; the ICRC is still looking for effective compliance systems.

cases.name: Nicaragua v Germany (provisional measures)
cases.holding: The request was rejected because the conditions weren't met on the evidence (Germany had reduced exports). The Court recalled all States' obligations under CA1 and the Genocide Convention regarding arms transfers.
cases.use: The external dimension of CA1 before the ICJ.

cases.name: R (Campaign Against Arms Trade) v Secretary of State
cases.court: England and Wales Court of Appeal
cases.holding: The government's decision to continue arms sales to Saudi Arabia was unlawful because it made no assessment of whether past IHL violations had occurred, which was relevant to the 'clear risk' test.
cases.use: Domestic enforcement of IHL through export controls.

cases.name: Bemba (Appeals)
cases.holding: Bemba's conviction under Art 28 was reversed. The Trial Chamber erred in assessing the 'necessary and reasonable measures' of a remote commander (and on the scope of charges).
cases.use: The limits of command responsibility.

cards.q: What does the external dimension of CA1 require?
cards.a: Negatively: not encourage, aid or assist violations by other parties (e.g. arms transfers knowing of a clear risk). Positively: take feasible measures to bring violations to an end, a due diligence standard (ICRC 2016).

cards.q: What are the elements of command responsibility under Art 28(a)?
cards.a: An underlying crime; effective control (and command or authority); knowledge or 'should have known'; failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent, repress or submit for prosecution; and the crimes resulted from the failure to exercise control properly (causation).

cards.q: What does the grave breaches regime require of States?
cards.a: Enact legislation with effective penal sanctions, search for persons alleged to have committed grave breaches regardless of nationality, and try them or hand them over (aut dedere aut judicare). Universal and mandatory, but only in IAC.

cards.q: Why did the ICRC–Swiss compliance initiative fail?
cards.a: States resisted a Meeting of States with reporting and thematic discussions, fearing politicisation and loss of control. The 32nd International Conference (2015) adopted only a weak process to continue talks.

cards.q: List the enforcement mechanisms of IHL from the lecture.
cards.a: Reciprocity; reprisals (heavily restricted); public opinion; Chapter VII; Protecting Powers and the ICRC; the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (API Art 90); State responsibility (reparation, API Art 91) and individual criminal responsibility (grave breaches, war crimes).

cards.q: What are the limits of the IHFFC?
cards.a: Competence only if States accepted it (in advance or ad hoc); only States can request an enquiry; no right of initiative; it establishes facts and does not make legal assessments. It was used for the first time in Eastern Ukraine at the OSCE's request.

cards.q: When are belligerent reprisals still lawful?
cards.a: Only in IAC, against persons and objects not protected by treaty or custom, as a last resort, proportionate and after warning (ICRC Rule 145). Prohibited against GC-protected persons and objects (Rules 146–147) and entirely in NIAC (Rule 148).

cards.q: What conditions did States impose on any new IHL compliance forum (Pejic)?
cards.a: State-driven and consensus-based; voluntary and non-binding; non-politicised, non-contextual (no naming specific conflicts) and non-selective; universal and impartial; no new legal obligations and no reconfiguring of existing mechanisms. The result, Resolution 2 (2015), only continued talks. Contrast IHRL's reporting and complaint systems.

excerpts.text: The High Contracting Parties undertake to respect and to ensure respect for the present Convention in all circumstances.
excerpts.why: Internal and external dimension: a due diligence duty on third States (ICRC 2016 Commentary; Wall para 158).

topics.title: The right to life in war and peace
core: ICCPR Art 6: no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of life. HRC GC 36: arbitrariness includes unlawfulness, inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process, and unreasonableness, necessity and proportionality.

Peacetime use of lethal force: only as a last resort, to protect life or prevent serious injury from an imminent threat. Strict necessity and proportionality (GC 36 para 12; the UN Basic Principles on Force and Firearms, Principle 9).

ECHR Art 2(2): force 'absolutely necessary' for the listed aims. McCann (Gibraltar): the soldiers' honest belief was justified, but the planning and control of the operation (letting the suspects enter, reliance on assumptions, shooting to kill) violated Art 2.

Positive obligations: a legal framework, operational measures (Osman), and the procedural duty to investigate (effective, independent, prompt, transparent, with victim involvement). It applies in armed conflict (Al-Skeini; Jaloud; GC 36 para 64; Minnesota Protocol). Armed groups controlling territory may also have to investigate (Niyo).

Death penalty: limited to the 'most serious crimes' (intentional killing). Abolitionist trend (Second Optional Protocol; ECHR Protocols 6 and 13). Non-refoulement where there is a real risk of the death penalty (Judge v Canada).

In armed conflict: practices consistent with IHL are generally not arbitrary (Nuclear Weapons para 25; GC 36 para 64). But GC 36 adds IHRL considerations, such as investigating, and nuclear weapons being incompatible with Art 6.

IHL targeting rules: distinction (combatants and military objectives versus civilians and civilian objects); civilians lose protection only for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities (API 51(3)). The ICRC Interpretive Guidance on DPH sets three cumulative criteria: threshold of harm, direct causation, and belligerent nexus. Members of organised armed groups with a continuous combat function are targetable at all times.

Proportionality (API 51(5)(b)): expected incidental civilian harm must not be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Precautions (API 57): feasible verification, choice of means, warnings, and cancelling attacks.

Persons hors de combat (API 41: surrender, wounded, in the power of the adversary) must not be attacked. Debate over the right to life of combatants: Rosenzweig, and Pictet's 'capture rather than kill' (least harmful means; the ICRC Guidance section IX).

The 2025 boat strikes (US strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific since 2 Sept 2025): there is no armed conflict with cartels (no Tadić intensity or organisation), so the IHRL law-enforcement paradigm applies, making them extrajudicial executions. States have a duty to investigate (Schmitt and Milanovic; O'Connell). This is a contemporary illustration of classification determining the applicable standard. Dated facts: the 2 Oct 2025 notice to Congress claimed a NIAC with 'unlawful combatants'; Türk (31 Oct 2025) found IHRL breaches; UN experts (Nov 2025) flagged possible international crimes; Congress inquired into the 2 Sept 'second strike' on survivors (Dec 2025); at least 223 killed in 68+ strikes by Sept 2026.

A 'right to survival'? Traditionally Art 6 ICCPR / Art 2 ECHR protect against killings, but there is a growing socio-economic dimension: CRC Art 6 links life with 'survival and development'; the IACtHR reads life as a right to a dignified existence; the African Commission (Ogoniland, SERAC v Nigeria) found environmental destruction violated the right to life; the ECtHR found a violation where emergency treatment was refused for inability to pay (Mehmet Şentürk and Bekir Şentürk v Turkey) but is reluctant to go further (Cyprus v Turkey left general health care open). Bantekas and Oette conclude States must take steps reasonably expected to ensure survival, including against environmental degradation (now GC 36 and the climate cases).

Capture before killing? Human rights courts have not required government forces in an armed conflict to try to arrest a fighter before using lethal force, but in lower-intensity counter-terrorism operations they insist on arrest rather than killing where feasible (Bantekas and Oette). This maps onto the paradigm split: conduct of hostilities versus law enforcement, and onto the ICRC Interpretive Guidance section IX debate.
lecture: The right to life protects against arbitrary taking; it is non-derogable but not absolute (Weeramantry: 'the irreducible core of human rights'). Provisions: ECHR Art 2, ICCPR Art 6, ACHR Art 4 (life 'in general, from the moment of conception'), ACHPR Art 4 ('human beings are inviolable').

Targeted killing is undefined in IL. Alston's definition: intentional, premeditated and deliberate use of lethal force by States or agents under colour of law, or by an organised armed group in armed conflict, against a specific individual not in the perpetrator's custody. Unlike 'extrajudicial execution', 'summary execution' or 'assassination' (illegal by definition), targeted killing may be lawful in armed conflict.

The answer depends on the framework. Law enforcement: lethal force only where absolutely necessary to protect persons from unlawful violence, a last resort when arrest is impossible, assessed case by case. Armed conflict: 'lethal force is the name of the game' — lawfulness turns on the target's status (combatant, fighter, DPH). 'War on terror' rhetoric is used to push the IHL framework.

ECHR Art 2(2): force no more than absolutely necessary for (a) defence from unlawful violence, (b) lawful arrest or preventing escape, (c) quelling a riot or insurrection. Kretzmer's two prongs: is force required at all, or could other measures protect the threatened persons? If so, is lethal force needed, or would lesser force do?

McCann (1995): an honest belief perceived for good reasons to be valid can justify force even if mistaken; but the decision not to stop the suspects entering Gibraltar, the failure to allow for intelligence errors, and the 'automatic recourse to lethal force' meant the killings were not absolutely necessary (para 213). The operation must be planned and controlled to minimise recourse to lethal force.

Tagayeva v Russia (Beslan, 2017): a real and immediate risk to schoolchildren was known; preventive measures were inadequate (Osman duty), the legal framework on lethal force was deficient, and the rescue operation's planning and control violated Art 2.

Strict necessity: Giuliani and Gaggio v Italy (2011) — 'absolute necessity' is stricter than 'necessary in a democratic society'. UN Basic Principles on Force and Firearms: restraint, proportionality to the seriousness of the offence, minimise damage, preserve life. IACHR Report on Terrorism: lethal force against suspects only where strictly unavoidable to protect from an imminent threat of death or serious injury.

Alston (paras 32–33): under IHRL a killing is lawful only if required to protect life (proportionality) and there is no other means such as capture or incapacitation (necessity). So an intentional, premeditated killing by law enforcement can never be lawful; a 'shoot-to-kill' policy violates IHRL.

In armed conflict a targeted killing is lawful only against combatants, civilians directly participating, or members with a continuous combat function, with distinction, proportionality and precautions. PCATI v Israel (2006) para 40: 'a rule-of-law state employs, to the extent possible, procedures of law and not procedures of force'. US practice blurs jus ad bellum (self-defence) and jus in bello.

Combatant status builds up in layers: armed forces; Hague Regs Art 1 (militias and volunteer corps with responsible command, a fixed distinctive sign, open arms, respect for the laws of war); Art 2 levée en masse (spontaneous resistance to invading troops, arms carried openly, respect for the laws of war — debated for armed Ukrainian citizens in 2022); GCIII Art 4A (forces of unrecognised governments, organised resistance movements). Civilians are defined negatively (API Art 50); in doubt, a person is a civilian; the presence of non-civilians does not change the population's civilian character.

DPH (API 51(3), APII 13(3)): 'unless and for such time'. ICRC Interpretive Guidance (2009): threshold of harm, direct causation (including as an integral part of a coordinated operation), belligerent nexus. Continuous combat function: lasting integration into an organised armed group with an ongoing role preparing, executing or commanding hostile acts; recruitment, training and equipping can prove it; political, financial or propaganda roles do not; targetable while the function lasts, without combatant privilege.

Classroom case: Maya, a civilian, sends the precise coordinates of an enemy artillery unit at one party's request for an immediate attack — all three DPH criteria are met. Posting general support on social media is not DPH.

Drones and globalised targeted killing: which paradigm (armed conflict or law enforcement), compliance with IHL, the 'joystick mentality', what precautions are 'feasible'. Discussion film: 'Eye in the Sky' (the trolley dilemma).

cases.name: McCann v UK
cases.holding: The killing of three IRA suspects in Gibraltar violated Art 2 because of failures in the control and organisation of the operation, even though the soldiers believed in good faith that it was necessary.
cases.use: Absolute necessity; planning and control; the duty to investigate.

cases.name: HRC General Comment 36
cases.holding: A broad understanding of the right to life: the duty to investigate, positive obligations (environment, climate), extraterritorial application by impact (para 63), co-application with IHL (para 64), and the death penalty.
cases.use: The main IHRL source for any lethal force question.

cases.name: Jaloud v Netherlands
cases.holding: The Netherlands had jurisdiction over a checkpoint in Iraq under its command, and the investigation of the shooting of a civilian was inadequate (Art 2 procedural).
cases.use: The investigation duty in armed conflict; jurisdiction through checkpoints.

cases.name: Targeted Killings case (PCATI v Israel)
cases.holding: Civilians who directly participate in hostilities lose protection for such time; there must be reliable information, a less harmful means must be used if available (arrest), and there must be a retroactive investigation.
cases.use: DPH; the least harmful means.

cases.name: Tagayeva v Russia (Beslan)
cases.holding: Russia violated Art 2: it failed to take preventive measures despite specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to schoolchildren, had a deficient legal framework on the use of force, and the rescue operation (thermobaric weapons, tanks) was not planned and controlled to minimise loss of life.
cases.use: Positive obligations and planning of operations.

cases.name: Giuliani and Gaggio v Italy
cases.holding: Shooting of a protester at the Genoa G8: the officer acted in self-defence, but the Court restated that 'absolutely necessary' requires a stricter, more compelling test than 'necessary in a democratic society'.
cases.use: The strictness of Art 2(2).

cards.q: When may State agents use lethal force in peacetime?
cards.a: Only when strictly unavoidable to protect life from an imminent threat, as a last resort, proportionate, with planning to minimise recourse to lethal force, followed by an effective investigation (GC 36; Basic Principles; McCann).

cards.q: What are the three ICRC criteria for direct participation in hostilities?
cards.a: Threshold of harm (likely to adversely affect military operations or cause death, injury or destruction); direct causation (one causal step); belligerent nexus (specifically designed to support a party to the detriment of another).

cards.q: How does GC 36 deal with armed conflict?
cards.a: Art 6 continues to apply. Uses of lethal force consistent with IHL and other applicable IL norms are, in general, not arbitrary, but States must still investigate potentially unlawful deaths and disclose criteria (para 64).

cards.q: What are the elements of a proportionality assessment in attack?
cards.a: Expected incidental loss of civilian life, injury, or damage to civilian objects, weighed against the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Unlawful if excessive (API 51(5)(b), 57(2)(a)(iii); Rome 8(2)(b)(iv) 'clearly excessive').

cards.q: Why do the 2025 boat strikes matter?
cards.a: Classification determines the law. Absent an armed conflict, IHRL law enforcement standards apply, under which the strikes are unlawful killings. Calling cartels 'unlawful combatants' cannot create an armed conflict. It also triggers the duty to investigate.

cards.q: What are Kretzmer's two prongs for lethal force under Art 2?
cards.a: (1) Is the use of force absolutely required, or could other measures protect the threatened persons? (2) If force is required, is it absolutely necessary to use lethal force, or would a lesser degree suffice?

cards.q: Why can a targeted killing never be lawful under IHRL (Alston)?
cards.a: Lethal force is lawful only when strictly and directly necessary to save life from an imminent threat, with no alternative such as capture. In a law-enforcement operation killing can never be the sole objective; a premeditated killing plan, or a shoot-to-kill policy, is therefore unlawful.

cards.q: When does a civilian with a continuous combat function lose protection, and what don't they get?
cards.a: While integrated in an organised armed group with an ongoing role preparing, executing or commanding hostile acts, they are targetable at any time, including between operations. They have no combatant privilege or POW status and can be prosecuted for participating.

topics.title: Liberty, detention and fair trial
core: ICCPR Art 9 (no arbitrary arrest or detention; reasons, prompt appearance before a judge, habeas corpus, compensation; GC 35). ECHR Art 5 (an exhaustive list of permitted grounds in 5(1)(a)–(f); safeguards in 5(2)–(5)).

Arbitrariness is broader than unlawfulness: inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability, necessity and proportionality (GC 35 para 12). Security detention outside criminal proceedings is extremely limited in peacetime.
Positive obligations: protection against slavery and trafficking (Rantsev), refugees and migrants (immigration detention as a last resort; no detention of children), and enforced disappearance.
Fair trial (ICCPR Art 14; ECHR Art 6): an independent and impartial tribunal, presumption of innocence, defence rights. The core is non-derogable in practice (GC 29, GC 32).

IAC: POWs may be interned until the end of active hostilities (GCIII 21, 118) without individual review. Civilians may be interned only if 'absolutely necessary' for security (GCIV 42) or for 'imperative reasons of security' in occupation (78), with initial and six-monthly review.

NIAC: CA3 and APII protect detainees (humane treatment, fair trial by a 'regularly constituted court'), but there is no explicit legal basis for internment. Serdar Mohammed: the High Court (Leggatt J, 2014) held that NIAC IHL gives no power to detain. The UK Supreme Court (2017) found authority in the SC resolutions, left the IHL question open (the Justices were divided), and held that the review procedures fell short of Art 5(4). The ICRC says custom implicitly permits it. Plemanac and Teferra on the limits of security detention.
Co-application: Hassan v UK (IAC internment compatible with Art 5 read in light of IHL, without derogation). For NIAC, derogation is probably needed, or an IHRL legal basis.

Extraordinary rendition and black sites (Duffy): shared responsibility of host and complicit States. El-Masri v FYROM (2012): torture, enforced disappearance and arbitrary detention. Al Nashiri and Abu Zubaydah v Poland (2014): Poland's complicity in CIA black sites; Art 3 and Art 5 violations, risk of the death penalty.
Detention by non-state armed groups: obligations under CA3 (humane treatment), and the ICRC's push for standards.

Administrative (preventive) detention is not expressly prohibited by IHRL but is detention without trial, so it must be prescribed by law, necessary for a legitimate aim and subject to continuous judicial review; prolonged detention without trial has been argued to be ill-treatment in itself. In practice it is used to stifle opposition and was revived in counter-terrorism (Guantánamo, Belmarsh). Example: Israel's Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law 2002 (14 days without judicial review, lawyer access restricted up to 7 days, renewable 6-month orders) and Military Order 1651 for the West Bank (96 hours without review; 6-month renewable orders on undefined 'regional or public security'; classified evidence). Even under IHL such detention must be exceptional (GCIV 78).

Military and special courts: the HRC still allows military courts to try civilians in exceptional cases (GC 32 para 22), but HRC member Salvioli (Akwanga v Cameroon, 2011) argues that only an absolute ban is compatible with ICCPR Art 14, given the history of courts-martial used against political opponents and to shield soldiers. The African Commission (Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v Egypt, 2011, State Security Emergency Court, torture-based confessions, no appeal) held that tribunals not using duly established procedures 'shall not be created to displace the jurisdiction' of ordinary courts. Relevant to Guantánamo military commissions and to CA3's 'regularly constituted court'.
lecture: Five questions for any detention problem: (1) applicable law (IAC, NIAC, none; which IHRL obligations); (2) status of the detainee; (3) authority and grounds; (4) treatment; (5) review and release.

IHRL baseline: ICCPR Art 9 (legal basis, not arbitrary); ECHR Art 5(1) (enumerated grounds only); safeguards: reasons, prompt judicial control in criminal cases, habeas corpus. Detention review (ICCPR 9(4), ECHR 5(4): may the person remain detained?) is distinct from a criminal trial (ICCPR 14, ECHR 6: did they commit an offence?). Security internment does not establish guilt.

Context: the US Military Order of 13 November 2001 — detention and military commissions for non-citizens designated by the President, with an express denial of any remedy in any court, domestic, foreign or international.
Arbitrary detention is prohibited in IAC and NIAC (ICRC customary Rule 99) — here IHL and IHRL are in harmony. Internment is preventive; punishment requires separate proceedings.

IAC: GCI and II (medical and religious personnel), GCIII (POWs until the end of hostilities; Art 13 humane treatment, no reprisals, protection from public curiosity), GCIV Arts 42–43 ('absolutely necessary', regular review) and Art 78 (imperative security reasons, appeal and review in occupation); API Art 75 (prompt reasons in a language understood) as a minimum standard for all situations. Unlawful confinement is a grave breach (GCIV Art 147).

NIAC: the prohibition of arbitrary detention is customary; Duffy — 'detention is not an alternative to criminal law'; whether NIAC IHL itself authorises internment is contested (Akande; Serdar Mohammed, High Court 2014). CA3 binds organised armed groups too. The ICRC seeks consensus rules, as with DPH. Open question: apply IAC rules by analogy, or IHRL undiluted because there is no lex specialis? Is undiluted IHRL realistic for 'battlefield detention'?

Guantánamo: no POW status for anyone, more than two years without an Art 5 'competent tribunal', 5 m² cells, sleep deprivation, no lawyers. A 'legal black hole'? Under the IAC framework everyone is either a combatant (GCIII) or a civilian (GCIV, subject to its Art 4 nationality conditions), with IHRL as the floor. Combatant criteria: membership of armed forces or integrated militias, or militias meeting the four Hague conditions (applied to the Taliban and al-Qaeda). Location and type of conflict matter.

IHRL on security detention: a margin of appreciation for terrorism suspects, but pre-trial detention is the exception (Duffy); derogation must be necessary and proportionate; detention must never be arbitrary, unacknowledged or prolonged, and needs safeguards. Abu Zubaydah v Poland (2014) para 523: terrorism gives no carte blanche under Art 5; also Al-Hawsawi v Lithuania (2024).

US courts: Rasul v Bush (2004) and Boumediene v Bush (2008) secured habeas review in the DC District Court; Combatant Status Review Tribunals gave way to Administrative and then Periodic Review Boards.

Hassan v UK (GC 2014): Tarek Hassan was captured armed with intelligence documents and held at Camp Bucca. The UK argued jurisdiction should not apply in active hostilities (para 76); the Court refused, citing the ICJ on concurrent application (para 77). The lack of a derogation does not prevent taking IHL into account when interpreting Art 5 (paras 102–103), but safeguards remain (para 104): a legal basis in IHL, competent body review, no arbitrariness.

cases.name: Hassan v UK (GC)
cases.holding: In an IAC, internment authorised by GCIII and GCIV may be accommodated within Art 5 even though it is not among the listed grounds, provided there is a legal basis, protection against arbitrariness, and review.
cases.use: Co-application in detention.

cases.name: El-Masri v FYROM (GC)
cases.holding: FYROM was responsible for the detention, ill-treatment amounting to torture (at Skopje airport by the CIA in the presence of Macedonian officials), and transfer to Afghanistan. It also violated the right to truth.
cases.use: Extraordinary rendition; complicity; torture.

cases.name: Serdar Mohammed v Ministry of Defence
cases.holding: UK forces in Afghanistan (NIAC) had authority to detain beyond 96 hours based on UNSC resolutions, but violated Art 5(4) by not providing adequate review. The Court was divided on whether IHL provides authority for NIAC detention.
cases.use: The legal basis for NIAC detention.

cases.name: Abu Zubaydah v Poland
cases.holding: Poland hosted a CIA black site and was responsible for the applicant's torture, secret detention and transfer. Terrorism investigations do not give authorities carte blanche under Art 5 (para 523).
cases.use: Complicity in rendition; Art 5 limits in counter-terrorism.

cases.name: Boumediene v Bush
cases.holding: Guantánamo detainees have the constitutional privilege of habeas corpus; the review procedure under the Detainee Treatment Act was an inadequate substitute.
cases.use: Ending the 'legal black hole'.

cards.q: What is the difference between POW internment and civilian internment in IAC?
cards.a: POWs: status-based, until the end of active hostilities, with no review needed (GCIII). Civilians: an exceptional security measure, 'absolutely necessary' or 'imperative reasons of security', individualised, with periodic review (GCIV 42–43, 78).

cards.q: Why is NIAC detention problematic?
cards.a: CA3 and APII regulate treatment but don't provide an explicit power to intern. IHRL requires a legal basis and judicial review, so States need domestic law, SC authorisation, or a derogation.

cards.q: What did Hassan decide, and why is it controversial?
cards.a: Art 5 is interpreted to accommodate IHL internment in IAC without derogation. Critics say the Court rewrote an exhaustive list and should have required Art 15 derogation.

cards.q: Which rights are violated by extraordinary rendition?
cards.a: Liberty (arbitrary and secret detention), torture and ill-treatment, enforced disappearance, the right to truth and to an effective remedy, and non-refoulement (risk of torture or the death penalty). Complicity of participating States (El-Masri; Al Nashiri).

cards.q: What are the five questions for any detention problem?
cards.a: (1) Applicable law: IAC, NIAC or none, and which IHRL obligations? (2) Status of the detainee. (3) Authority and grounds for detention. (4) Treatment and conditions. (5) Review and release: how can it be challenged, and when must it end?

cards.q: Detention review versus criminal trial?
cards.a: Review asks whether a person may lawfully remain detained and can lead to release (ICCPR 9(4), ECHR 5(4); GCIV 43, 78). A trial asks whether the person committed an offence and leads to acquittal or conviction (ICCPR 14, ECHR 6). Security internment never establishes guilt.

cards.q: When is administrative (security) detention compatible with IHRL?
cards.a: Only exceptionally: a clear legal basis, necessity for a legitimate aim, prompt and continuous judicial review with real access to the evidence and a lawyer, and no use as a substitute for criminal proceedings. Regimes with long periods without judicial control, undefined security grounds and classified evidence (e.g. Israel's 2002 Unlawful Combatants Law and Military Order 1651) fail these standards (Bantekas and Oette pp 710–712; Duffy: 'detention is not an alternative to criminal law').
