topics.title: Torture and ill-treatment; starvation and aid
core: The prohibition of torture is jus cogens and absolute (CAT; ICCPR Art 7; ECHR Art 3; Furundžija paras 153–157; Belgium v Senegal para 99). It is non-derogable and has no exceptions for terrorism or the 'ticking bomb' (Gäfgen v Germany: threatening a suspect to save a child's life was still inhuman treatment).

CAT Art 1: (1) severe pain or suffering, physical or mental, (2) intentionally inflicted, (3) for a purpose (information, confession, punishment, intimidation, discrimination), (4) by or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official.

The ECHR distinguishes torture from inhuman or degrading treatment by the severity of suffering and purpose (Ireland v UK 1978: the 'five techniques' were inhuman, not torture; Selmouni 1999: the threshold is lowered as a 'living instrument'). There is a minimum level of severity. Degrading treatment means humiliation.

ICL definitions: under the Rome Statute, torture as CAH (Art 7(2)(e)) requires custody or control and no purpose and no official requirement. As a war crime, the Elements require a purpose. Kunarac: no State actor requirement in ICL.
Rape and sexual violence can constitute torture (Aydın v Turkey; Akayesu; Furundžija; the CAT Committee). Bodily integrity.
Non-refoulement: absolute under Art 3 ECHR (Soering; Chahal; Saadi v Italy, no balancing against national security) and CAT Art 3. Diplomatic assurances need scrutiny (Othman).
'Enhanced interrogation' (waterboarding, stress positions) is torture or inhuman treatment. Black sites and complicity (above).
Ill-treatment of civilians in armed conflict: prohibition of acts or threats of violence whose primary purpose is to spread terror among the civilian population (API 51(2); Galić).

Starvation as a method of warfare is prohibited (API 54; APII 14; ICRC customary Rule 53), and it is a war crime in IAC (Rome Art 8(2)(b)(xxv)) and since 2019 in NIAC (8(2)(e)(xix)). Protection of objects indispensable to survival.

Humanitarian assistance: parties must allow and facilitate rapid and unimpeded passage of relief for civilians in need (API 70; GCIV 23; the occupant's duty in GCIV 55, 59). Consent to relief operations may not be arbitrarily withheld (Oxford Guidance). Denial of aid can contribute to starvation, CAH extermination, or genocide (conditions of life).

Famine determinations: the IPC Famine Review Committee confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate (22 Aug 2025, conditions as of 15 Aug), the first in the Middle East, 'entirely man-made'. Israel rejected it. Famine was confirmed in El Fasher and Kadugli, Sudan, on 3 Nov 2025. Relevance: starvation as a method of warfare (API 54; Rule 53; Rome Art 8(2)(b)(xxv), and in NIAC 8(2)(e)(xix)) and the duty to allow relief (GCIV 23, 55, 59; API 70). Compare the ICJ provisional measures in South Africa v Israel.

Gäfgen v Germany (GC 2010) in full: (1) the threat of severe pain was inhuman treatment, not torture; (2) the officers' suspended fines did not satisfy the procedural duty to punish Art 3 violations adequately; (3) the long delay on the compensation claim breached the right to an effective remedy; but (4) no Art 6 violation, even though the body was found because of the threat, because his final confession at trial was 'voluntary' (a 'break in the causal chain'). A strong dissent said absoluteness requires excluding all evidence obtained in breach. Bantekas and Oette: affirming absoluteness is 'only the first step'; the hard question is what legal consequences follow.

Non-state torturers: under CAT Art 1 torture needs a public official or someone acting with official consent or acquiescence, while ICL drops this (Kunarac). Human rights bodies bend the official requirement mainly through non-refoulement: sending someone to be tortured by a de facto authority can breach CAT Art 3 (e.g. Elmi v Australia, CAT 1999, Somali factions exercising quasi-governmental control). Bantekas and Oette: criminal tribunals ascribe liability whatever the offender's status, whereas human rights bodies need an element of State involvement.
lecture: The prohibition of torture and CIDT is absolute and jus cogens (ICCPR 7, ECHR 3, ACHPR 5). Three central elements in CAT Art 1: severe physical or mental suffering, a prohibited purpose, and official involvement. Torture is also a war crime (IAC and NIAC) and a crime against humanity where the context is met.
CAT Art 2(2): no exceptional circumstances whatsoever (war, threat of war, instability, emergency) justify torture. CAT Art 15: evidence obtained by torture is inadmissible.

Erosion after 9/11: Ben Saul — Amnesty received torture reports from over 150 States (1997–2000); US practice signalled acceptability and undermined the prohibition's universal normativity. Duffy: torture 'is not a novelty of the war on terror, it is a defining feature of it'.

CIDT threshold: a minimum level of severity, relative to nature, context, duration, physical and mental effects, and sometimes sex, age and health (Opuz v Turkey 2009). Ireland v UK: the five techniques were inhuman and degrading, not torture. Torture is distinguished by severity and purpose.

Positive and procedural obligations: no incommunicado detention; access to a lawyer, doctor, courts and third parties; criminalise (CAT Art 4), prosecute or extradite (Art 7), investigate promptly and impartially (Art 12), receive complaints (Art 13) and provide redress (Art 14); non-refoulement where there are substantial grounds to fear ill-treatment.

'Manufactured legality': the OLC memos (Gonzales, Bybee, Yoo). Bybee (1 Aug 2002): torture requires pain 'equivalent in intensity to … organ failure … or even death'. The follow-up memo listed 10 'legally acceptable' techniques: attention grasp, walling, facial hold, facial slap, cramped confinement, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation, insects in a box, waterboarding. Ticking-bomb arguments; black sites.

Extraordinary rendition (Babar Ahmad v UK (dec.), 6 July 2010, para 113; adopted in El-Masri GC 2012 para 221): an extra-judicial transfer for detention and interrogation outside the normal legal system where there is a real risk of ill-treatment. Duffy: 'the nadir of the descent to international illegality of the war on terror'. Features: authorisation at the highest level (the 17 Sept 2001 Memorandum of Notification; Cheney's 'dark side'), absolute secrecy, standardised 'enhanced interrogation', guaranteed impunity, ongoing violations, and multi-State complicity — a 'global spider's web'.

Abu Zubaydah v Poland para 524: secret detention aimed to remove detainees from any legal protection; host-State cooperation was the 'necessary condition' for black sites. Para 511: the treatment amounted to torture. Para 512: Poland 'facilitated the whole process' through 'acquiescence and connivance' and must have known the risk. Also Al Nashiri v Poland (2014), Abu Zubaydah v Lithuania and Al Nashiri v Romania (2018), El-Masri v Macedonia (2012).

Rights violated by rendition: liberty (unacknowledged detention is 'a complete negation' of liberty guarantees); torture and CIDT (including family members' anguish); enforced disappearance; non-refoulement (non-derogable, cannot be weighed against security; the flimsiness of diplomatic assurances — Babar Ahmad allowed extradition to a supermax with assurances); remedy and reparation; truth and the duty to investigate.
Responses: State responsibility for aid or assistance (ARSIWA Art 16: knowledge plus a close causal link), human rights litigation, individual criminal responsibility (ICC, universal jurisdiction).

cases.name: Ireland v UK
cases.holding: The 'five techniques' (wall-standing, hooding, noise, sleep deprivation, food and drink deprivation) were inhuman and degrading but did not reach the 'special stigma' of torture. Revision was refused in 2018.
cases.use: The torture versus inhuman treatment distinction (and its evolution).

cases.name: Selmouni v France
cases.holding: Severe police beatings amounted to torture. The Convention is a living instrument, and increasingly high standards mean acts once classed as inhuman may now be torture.
cases.use: The evolving threshold.

cases.name: Gäfgen v Germany (GC)
cases.holding: Police threatened a kidnapping suspect with severe pain to locate the child. This was inhuman treatment and absolutely prohibited, whatever the motive.
cases.use: The ticking bomb and absoluteness.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Furundžija
cases.holding: The prohibition of torture is jus cogens, with consequences including universal jurisdiction and the invalidity of amnesties. Rape can constitute torture.
cases.use: Jus cogens; sexual violence.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Galić
cases.holding: The campaign of sniping and shelling in Sarajevo was terror against the civilian population, a war crime (primary purpose to spread terror).
cases.use: Terrorising civilians.

cases.name: Abu Zubaydah v Poland / Al Nashiri v Poland
cases.holding: Poland hosted a CIA black site; the treatment amounted to torture; Poland was responsible through acquiescence and connivance, for secret detention (Art 5), and for failing to investigate (procedural Art 3); also for exposing the applicants to the risk of further ill-treatment and an unfair trial.
cases.use: Complicity in rendition; positive obligations.

cases.name: Opuz v Turkey
cases.holding: The State failed to protect a woman and her mother from repeated domestic violence despite knowledge of the risk (Arts 2, 3 and 14: gender-based discrimination). Ill-treatment must reach a relative minimum level of severity.
cases.use: The CIDT threshold; due diligence against private violence.

cases.name: Babar Ahmad v UK
cases.holding: Extradition to the US (possible supermax detention, life without parole) did not violate Art 3. The definition of extraordinary rendition ('an extra-judicial transfer … for the purposes of detention and interrogation outside the normal legal system, where there was a real risk of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment') comes from the earlier admissibility decision, Babar Ahmad v UK (dec.), 6 July 2010, para 113, which relied on US assurances (no rendition, no death penalty, no military commission). The 2012 judgment held that detention at ADX Florence and life sentences would not breach Art 3.
cases.use: Definition of rendition; diplomatic assurances.

cards.q: What are the four elements of torture under CAT Art 1?
cards.a: Severe physical or mental pain or suffering; intentionally inflicted; for a specified purpose; by, at the instigation of, or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or person acting in an official capacity.

cards.q: How do ICL definitions of torture differ from CAT?
cards.a: There is no official-capacity requirement (Kunarac). For CAH under the Rome Statute there is no purpose requirement, only custody or control. For war crimes, the Elements require a purpose.

cards.q: What does Gäfgen say about the ticking bomb?
cards.a: Even to save a life, threats of torture are prohibited. Art 3 is absolute and not subject to balancing.

cards.q: What legal framework applies to starvation and humanitarian access?
cards.a: API 54 and APII 14 prohibit starvation as a method of warfare; Rome 8(2)(b)(xxv) and (e)(xix) make it a war crime. API 70 and GCIV 23, 55, 59 require allowing and facilitating relief. Consent may not be arbitrarily withheld.

cards.q: What were the Bybee memo's torture standard and the 10 'acceptable' techniques?
cards.a: Pain equivalent to that accompanying serious physical injury such as organ failure or death. The techniques: attention grasp, walling, facial hold, facial slap, cramped confinement, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation, insects in a confinement box, waterboarding. Used to argue the CIA programme was not 'torture'.

cards.q: How did the ECtHR hold Poland responsible in Abu Zubaydah?
cards.a: Not by attributing CIA acts to Poland, but through its own conduct: it knew or must have known of the serious risk, hosted and facilitated the black site ('acquiescence and connivance', para 512), so it was responsible for torture (Art 3), secret detention (Art 5), the transfer, and failing to investigate.

cards.q: What did Gäfgen decide on evidence obtained through the threat of torture, and why is it criticised?
cards.a: The Grand Chamber found no Art 6 violation: the real evidence (the boy's body) was used, but the conviction rested on Gäfgen's later 'voluntary' confession at trial, which broke the causal chain. The dissent called this artificial: absoluteness requires excluding all evidence obtained in breach of Art 3. Bantekas and Oette suggest the Court may have been influenced by the prospect of a retrial and public outcry in Germany.

excerpts.text: No exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked as a justification of torture.
excerpts.why: Absolute and non-derogable; jus cogens (Belgium v Senegal para 99).

topics.title: The crime of aggression
core: From Nuremberg's 'crimes against peace' ('the supreme international crime') to the Rome Statute Art 5, with the definition deferred to Kampala (2010). Activation took effect on 17 July 2018 (ASP decision of December 2017).

Art 8 bis(1), the crime: planning, preparation, initiation or execution, by a person in a position effectively to exercise control over or to direct the political or military action of a State, of an act of aggression which by its character, gravity and scale constitutes a manifest violation of the UN Charter.

Art 8 bis(2), the act of aggression: the use of armed force by a State against the sovereignty, territorial integrity or political independence of another State (from GA Res 3314). Lists invasion, bombardment, blockade, attack on armed forces, sending armed bands, and so on.
Leadership element: a leadership crime only. Ordinary soldiers are not liable (Dannenbaum argues soldiers fighting in illegal wars are wronged and their killing of enemies is not 'innocent').
State act requirement: there must be an act of aggression by a State. Non-state actors' force against States is excluded (debated).

'Manifest violation' threshold: all three of character, gravity and scale must be sufficient (understanding 7). This excludes grey areas such as arguable humanitarian intervention or anticipatory self-defence.

Jurisdictional regime: Art 15 bis (State referral and proprio motu) excludes nationals of non-parties and crimes on their territory (Art 15 bis(5)). Parties may opt out (15 bis(4)). The 2017 ASP decision (Zimmermann; Kress) adopted the restrictive reading: no jurisdiction over nationals of States parties that haven't ratified the amendment. Art 15 ter: an SC referral has no such limits.

Effective inoperability: Russia isn't a party, and the SC is vetoed, so the ICC can't prosecute aggression against Ukraine. Hence the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine: CoE–Ukraine Agreement 25 June 2025, Rada ratification 15 July 2025, Enlarged Partial Agreement on the Management Committee (CM/Res(2026)5, 15 May 2026, 36 States plus the EU), seat in The Hague. Statute: no functional immunity (Art 23(4)); a sitting troika member's indictment cannot be confirmed until they leave office or immunity is waived (Art 23(5)/25(2)); limited trials in absentia with retrial right (Art 28). The July 2025 special session failed to harmonise Art 15 bis (Res ICC-ASP/S-1/Res.1; reconvene 2029).
The domestic route: Ukrainian and other national prosecutions (aggression as a domestic crime), but immunity issues persist for leaders.

Kress contrasts Nuremberg's 'supreme international crime' (aggression) with the later case law's description of genocide as the 'crime of crimes'. The shift reflects the move from a State-sovereignty-oriented to a human-being-oriented approach (Tadić para 97). Aggression necessarily violates international peace; genocide may stay within one State. Whether Nuremberg's ranking still holds depends on whether international peace and security remains the primary value of the international legal order. Good opening for an essay on aggression's place among the core crimes.
lecture: Opening hypothetical (Heinsch): State A invades State B to annex territory but its soldiers fully comply with IHL. Does that remove responsibility for aggression? Must the victim State comply with IHL? Who is responsible — the President, a commander, every soldier? Lesson: keep jus ad bellum and jus in bello separate. Ferencz on why States long avoided a definition.

Progression: League Covenant (Arts 10, 12–15: cooling-off, no comprehensive ban) → Kellogg-Briand 1928 (renunciation, no enforcement) → Charter Art 2(4) with Chapter VII and Art 51. IMT Charter Art 6(a): crimes against peace (planning, preparation, initiation or waging aggressive war) — addressing resort to war, while war crimes address its conduct; a legacy of legality concerns and selectivity.
Art 39 opens Chapter VII but does not establish individual guilt. GA Res 3314 (14 Dec 1974) defined aggression for the SC (Art 1, Art 3 list); Art 8 bis(2) imports it into criminal law.

Road to Kampala: Rome 1998 (in Art 5 but undefined) → Preparatory Commission → Special Working Group 2002–09 → Kampala Review Conference 2010, adopted by consensus (Annex I amendments incl. Art 25(3 bis); Annex II Elements; Annex III Understandings 6 and 7). Activation conditions: 30 ratifications (Palestine the 30th, 29 June 2016; now 45), after 1 Jan 2017, ASP decision 14 Dec 2017; active from 17 July 2018.

Elements: planning, preparation, initiation or execution (no need to fire a weapon); the completed crime needs a committed State act of aggression. Leadership is functional — effective control over or direction of a State's political or military action; title alone neither proves nor is required (industrialists or religious leaders could qualify). Art 25(3 bis) limits all modes of liability to leaders.

Should soldiers be liable? Dannenbaum: the wrong includes unjustified killing, supporting protection for those who refuse to fight; soldiers remain responsible for their own war crimes whichever side.

Non-state actors: Art 8 bis requires force by a State against a State; independent armed groups don't qualify; State-linked groups fall under (2)(g); the individual must still meet the leadership test.

Manifest violation: character (nature and legal context), gravity (seriousness and consequences), scale (magnitude and duration), assessed objectively and together. Understanding 7: 'no one component can be significant enough to satisfy the manifest standard by itself'; Understanding 6: consider all circumstances. Borderline cases (brief incursions, disputed legal bases, humanitarian motives) fall below; State responsibility may remain.

Mental element: Art 30 intent and knowledge; awareness of the facts establishing Charter inconsistency and the manifest violation (Elements 4 and 6); the accused need not have evaluated the law correctly; 'manifest' is objective.
Kampala's trade-off: agreement on a fourth core crime and an SC compromise, but legal-certainty concerns (a definition built on Res 3314 plus 'manifest') under Art 22's strict construction.

Jurisdiction: Art 15 bis (State referral, proprio motu) — non-parties excluded (15 bis(5)), and the 2017 activation resolution excludes States Parties that have not accepted the amendments; opt-out under 15 bis(4); the Prosecutor must first check for an SC determination and notify the SG; without one in six months the Pre-Trial Division may authorise (15 bis(8)); Art 16 deferral remains; external determinations do not bind the Court. Art 15 ter: SC referral without those consent limits, but subject to veto politics.

cases.name: IMT Nuremberg — crimes against peace
cases.holding: 'To initiate a war of aggression is not only an international crime; it is the supreme international crime, differing only from other war crimes in that it contains within itself the accumulated evil of the whole.'
cases.use: The historical foundation and gravity.

cases.name: Kampala amendments and the 2017 ASP activation
cases.holding: Defined the crime and act of aggression and set the consent-based jurisdiction regime. The 2017 activation confirmed that the Court has no jurisdiction over nationals or territory of States parties that haven't accepted the amendments.
cases.use: The jurisdictional limits; why Ukraine needs a special tribunal.

cases.name: Special session on the review of the aggression amendments (Res ICC-ASP/S-1/Res.1)
cases.holding: No consensus to harmonise Art 15 bis with the other crimes (removing the non-party exclusion and opt-out). States committed to 'strengthening' jurisdiction, annexed the proposal and convened a new special session in 2029.
cases.use: Why the Art 15 bis(5) gap persists; justification for the Special Tribunal.

cards.q: What are the elements of the crime of aggression (Art 8 bis)?
cards.a: Conduct: planning, preparation, initiation or execution. Perpetrator: a leader effectively able to control or direct State political or military action. An act of aggression by a State, which by its character, gravity and scale is a manifest violation of the Charter. Mental element: awareness of the factual circumstances.

cards.q: Why can't the ICC try Russian leaders for aggression against Ukraine?
cards.a: Art 15 bis(5) excludes nationals of non-States parties under State referral and proprio motu triggers. An SC referral (Art 15 ter) is blocked by Russia's veto.

cards.q: What is the 'manifest violation' threshold?
cards.a: Character, gravity and scale must together justify a manifest designation. It filters out legally contested uses of force (e.g. arguable self-defence or humanitarian intervention).

cards.q: Should ordinary soldiers be liable for aggression?
cards.a: The current law says no (leadership element). Dannenbaum argues soldiers in an aggressive war have their own moral and legal claims (selective conscientious objection, recognition as victims). The traditional equality of belligerents (jus in bello) separates conduct from the legality of war.

cards.q: What does Understanding 7 add to the 'manifest violation' test?
cards.a: Character, gravity and scale must together justify a 'manifest' determination, and 'no one component can be significant enough to satisfy the manifest standard by itself' — a combined, objective assessment.

cards.q: When did ICC jurisdiction over aggression become active, and how?
cards.a: 30 ratifications reached on 29 June 2016 (Palestine); the ASP decided on 14 December 2017 after the 1 January 2017 threshold; jurisdiction active from 17 July 2018. 45 States have ratified the amendments.

cards.q: Can the victim of aggression ignore IHL?
cards.a: No. Jus in bello applies equally to all parties regardless of who started the war (the equality of belligerents; API preamble). Compliance with IHL also does not cure an unlawful resort to force.

cards.q: How does the Ukraine Special Tribunal deal with immunity and absent accused?
cards.a: Functional immunity does not apply (Art 23(4)). For a sitting Head of State, Head of Government or Foreign Minister, investigation and an indictment are possible, but confirmation is suspended until they leave office or immunity is waived (Art 23(5), 25(2)); no measures of constraint (Art 24(4)). Trials in absentia are allowed under strict conditions, with a right to retrial (Art 28(3)). The Tribunal is grounded in Ukraine's territorial jurisdiction (Art 1), delegated via a CoE treaty.

topics.title: War crimes
core: Definition (Tadić Jurisdiction para 94): a serious violation of a rule of IHL (treaty or custom) that protects important values and entails individual criminal responsibility under IL.

Rome Art 8 structure: (2)(a) grave breaches of the GCs (IAC); (2)(b) other serious violations in IAC; (2)(c) serious violations of CA3 (NIAC); (2)(e) other serious violations in NIAC. Art 8(1): jurisdiction 'in particular' when committed as part of a plan or policy or large-scale commission (a gravity filter, not an element).

Contextual elements (Elements of Crimes): (1) the conduct took place in the context of and was associated with an armed conflict (nexus: Kunarac, the conflict 'played a substantial part' in the perpetrator's ability, decision or manner); (2) awareness of the factual circumstances establishing armed conflict; (3) the victims are protected persons (for grave breaches) or not taking active part in hostilities.

Categories (Robinson and Cryer): against persons (wilful killing, torture, hostage-taking, outrages on personal dignity, rape and sexual violence, child soldiers under 15 per Lubanga); attacks on prohibited targets (civilians, civilian objects, humanitarian personnel, protected buildings such as hospitals and cultural property, per Al Mahdi); excessive incidental damage (8(2)(b)(iv), 'clearly excessive', IAC only); property (pillage, destruction not justified by military necessity); prohibited means (poison, chemical and biological weapons, expanding bullets); prohibited methods (perfidy, starvation, no quarter, human shields).
Differences between IAC and NIAC have narrowed through custom (Tadić para 127) and amendments (2010, 2017, 2019). Gaps remain in the Rome Statute: disproportionate attacks only in IAC.
Modes of liability: commission (Art 25(3)(a), co-perpetration with control over the crime, per Lubanga), ordering, aiding and abetting, common purpose (25(3)(d)), and command responsibility (Art 28).

Command responsibility: effective control, knowledge or 'should have known', failure to take necessary and reasonable measures, causation (ICC). The ICTY lacked the causation requirement (Čelebići; Halilović).

Hathaway et al. 'What is a War Crime?': there is no comprehensive definition, and the categories are inconsistent across instruments. They propose a test. Meron: international tribunals' contribution to war crimes law (the expansion to NIAC, the role of custom). Mettraux traces the history of the law of war crimes (Leipzig to Nuremberg to the ad hoc tribunals).

Mettraux's definition: a war crime is 'a serious violation of the laws or customs of war for which the perpetrator incurs individual criminal responsibility as a direct result of the operation of international law', with three elements: an armed conflict (including occupation), a violation of IHL with a nexus to that conflict, and international criminalisation. The history is 'layered': limits on war, then customs, then laws, then crimes; responsibility moved from sovereigns to individuals, in roughly seven phases from the 12th century to the post-1990s tribunals. Conclusion: war crimes are 'the point at which IHL meets international criminal law'.

Meron on legality: Nuremberg had to rely on custom because the 1929 Geneva Convention did not apply on the eastern front, the Hague Convention's si omnes clause was contested, and neither treaty expressly criminalised its violations. The ILC's 1994 draft simply referred to 'crimes under general international law', whereas the Rome Statute lists and defines each crime, including those applicable in NIAC. This 'specificity approach', reinforced by the Elements and the tribunals' detailed case law, 'harmonizes more closely with the principle of nullum crimen' and is now ascendant.

Defences: duress and superior orders. In Erdemović (ICTY Appeals 1997) the majority held duress is no complete defence to killing innocent civilians (only mitigation). Cassese, dissenting, said the law 'should not set intractable standards' demanding martyrdom. Rome Art 31(1)(d) now allows duress as a full defence where there is a threat of imminent death or serious bodily harm, the person acts necessarily and reasonably to avoid it and does not intend greater harm than the one avoided. Superior orders (Art 33) are a defence only if the person was legally obliged to obey, did not know the order was unlawful and it was not manifestly unlawful; orders to commit genocide or CAH are always manifestly unlawful. Contrast the IMT and ICTY: mitigation only.
lecture: History: the 1919 Commission on the Responsibility of the Authors of the War; Nuremberg Charter Art 6(b) (murder, ill-treatment or deportation of civilians, murder of POWs, killing hostages, plunder, wanton destruction not justified by military necessity); ICTY Art 2 (grave breaches) and Art 3 (laws or customs of war); ICTR Art 4 (CA3 and APII violations).

Tadić's three-part formulation: a serious infringement (a rule protecting important values, grave consequences for the victim), a customary or applicable treaty rule, and individual criminal responsibility. Non-serious example: a combatant taking a loaf of bread in an occupied village (Hague Regs Art 46(1)).

Contextual elements: (I) an armed conflict exists (Tadić definition, covering inter-State, government v group, and group v group); (II) classification, because it decides which list applies — Hadžihasanović: what is a war crime in IAC is not necessarily one in NIAC; (III) nexus. Art 8(1)'s 'plan or policy or large-scale commission' is a jurisdictional guide, not a customary element.

IAC types: CA2 (Pictet: 'the respect due to human personality is not measured by the number of victims'; but a specific intention by one State to engage another — border incidents are debated; Wilmshurst: classification is often subjective in practice); occupation (CA2(2), Hague Regs 42); wars of national liberation (API Art 1(4), with a unilateral declaration to the Swiss depositary — the Polisario Front in 2015).

NIAC types: CA3 (intensity and organisation, distinct from riots and banditry); APII (State forces involved, organised groups under responsible command with territorial control enabling sustained operations; not riots or sporadic violence) — CA3 keeps an autonomous existence. Rome Art 8(2)(f): CA3-level threshold plus 'protracted' (Delalić). Cross-border NIACs against groups in an 'unwilling or unable' host (Solis) remain controversial.

Tadić's 'revolutionary moment' (1995): customary law criminalises serious CA3 violations, shown by State practice, national prosecutions, military manuals and unanimous SC resolutions (e.g. on Somalia).

Foreign intervention in a NIAC: on the government's side, the conflict stays internal; on the rebels' side, a 'double qualification' (IAC and NIAC in parallel). Indirect intervention: Tadić Appeals overall control (organising, coordinating or planning plus financing, training, equipping — no specific orders needed).

Nexus: Tadić ('an obvious link'); Kunarac — the conflict must have played a substantial part in the perpetrator's ability, decision, manner or purpose. Indicators: perpetrator is a combatant; victim a non-combatant or member of the opposing party; the act serves the military campaign; committed as part of official duties.

Six categories: crimes against non-combatants; attacks on prohibited targets (religious, cultural, medical); attacks causing excessive civilian damage; crimes against property (pillage); prohibited means (poison, chemical and biological weapons); prohibited methods (starvation, terror, child soldiers).

Art 8 as adopted in 1998 listed 34 acts for IAC (8(2)(a): 8; (b): 26) and 16 for NIAC ((c): 4; (e): 12). The 2010 Kampala amendment added three weapons crimes to (e) (giving the slides' 19), the 2017 amendments added three weapons crimes to both (b) and (e), and the 2019 amendment added starvation to (e)(xix). The amendments bind only ratifying States. The Elements of Crimes, drafted by States, aim at certainty and curb judicial creativity.

What you must prove: (1) an armed conflict; (2) its nature; (3) a protected person or object (not needed for sexual violence); (4) nexus; (5) actus reus; (6) mens rea — intent and knowledge under Art 30 unless otherwise provided.

Lecture 18 recap of IHL core principles as war crimes (Heinsch): Art 8(2)(b)(i) attacks on civilians ('distinction persons'), (ii) civilian objects ('distinction objects'), (iii) humanitarian or peacekeeping missions, (iv) clearly excessive incidental harm or widespread, long-term and severe environmental damage ('proportionality'), (v) undefended towns, (xx) weapons causing superfluous injury, if comprehensively prohibited and annexed. Note: there is no war crime for failing to take precautions.

Military objectives (API 52(2); ICRC Rule 8): by nature, location, purpose or use making an effective contribution to military action, whose destruction, capture or neutralisation offers a definite military advantage in the circumstances ruling at the time. Civilian objects are defined negatively (52(1)); in doubt, a normally civilian object such as a school or place of worship is presumed not to be used militarily (52(3)).

Indiscriminate attacks (API 51(4)(a)–(c); Rules 11–12): not directed at a specific military objective, or using means that cannot be directed or whose effects cannot be limited. Area bombardment treating separate objectives as one in a populated area is prohibited (51(5)(a)).

Proportionality (API 51(5)(b)): two problems flagged — comparing unlike values (no numerical formula for 'excessive') and judging under uncertainty (based on information reasonably available before the attack, not the outcome). Broad State interpretations may be one of the biggest causes of civilian casualties.

Precautions in attack (API 57) and against the effects of attack (API 58). Unnecessary suffering (API 35(1)–(2)): the choice of means is not unlimited; 35(3) widespread, long-term and severe environmental damage.

cards.q: What are the four Tadić conditions for a war crime?
cards.a: (1) A violation of a rule of IHL; (2) the rule is customary or applicable treaty law; (3) the violation is serious (breaches a rule protecting important values, with grave consequences); (4) it entails individual criminal responsibility under IL.

cards.q: What are the contextual elements of war crimes under the Rome Statute?
cards.a: The conduct took place in the context of and was associated with an IAC or NIAC (nexus); the perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances establishing armed conflict; protected status of the victims or objects.

cards.q: Name the four subsections of Rome Art 8(2).
cards.a: (a) grave breaches (IAC); (b) other serious violations of the laws and customs (IAC); (c) serious violations of CA3 (NIAC); (e) other serious violations (NIAC).

cards.q: Which war crime exists in IAC but not in NIAC in the Rome Statute, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Launching attacks knowing they will cause clearly excessive incidental civilian harm (8(2)(b)(iv)). In NIAC, prosecutors must rely on intentional attacks on civilians, a gap in protection.

cards.q: What six things must the Prosecutor prove for a war crime?
cards.a: (1) An armed conflict existed; (2) its character (IAC or NIAC), deciding which Art 8 list applies; (3) the victim or object was protected (except sexual violence); (4) a nexus to the conflict; (5) the actus reus; (6) the mens rea (Art 30 intent and knowledge unless otherwise provided).

cards.q: What are Kunarac's nexus indicators?
cards.a: The perpetrator is a combatant; the victim is a non-combatant; the victim belongs to the opposing party; the act serves the ultimate goal of a military campaign; the crime is committed as part of, or in the context of, the perpetrator's official duties.

cards.q: How is a NIAC classified when a foreign State intervenes?
cards.a: Intervening for the government: it remains a NIAC. Intervening for the rebels with its own troops: double qualification (an IAC between the States, a NIAC between government and rebels). Indirect intervention: if the State has overall control over the group (Tadić), the whole conflict becomes international.

cards.q: Is duress a defence to killing civilians?
cards.a: ICTY (Erdemović, Appeals 1997): not a complete defence to killing innocents, only mitigation; Cassese dissented ('intractable standards', martyrdom). ICC: yes, under Art 31(1)(d), if there is a threat of imminent death or serious bodily harm, the reaction is necessary and reasonable, and the person does not intend greater harm than the one sought to be avoided. Superior orders are separate (Art 33: limited defence, never for genocide or CAH).

cards.q: What are Mettraux's three elements of a war crime, and where do war crimes sit?
cards.a: (1) An armed conflict, including occupation; (2) conduct violating IHL with a nexus to that conflict; (3) international law criminalises it, so individual responsibility arises directly from international law. War crimes are 'the point at which IHL meets international criminal law': an extra criminal layer on top of core IHL prohibitions, born from the failure of reprisals and reparations as enforcement.

topics.title: Crimes against humanity
core: Rome Art 7(1) chapeau: any listed act committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of the attack.

'Attack' (Art 7(2)(a)): a course of conduct involving the multiple commission of listed acts against a civilian population, pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organisational policy. It need not be a military attack. No armed conflict nexus is required (Tadić; CCL 10).
Widespread means large-scale (number of victims or geographic scope). Systematic means organised nature, a pattern, non-accidental repetition (Kunarac). The test is disjunctive.

Civilian population: the population must be the primary object of the attack, predominantly civilian (the presence of some combatants doesn't change this). 'Any': nationality is irrelevant, including a State's own nationals.

Policy element: active promotion or encouragement by a State or organisation. The organisational policy debate (Kenya decision: the majority applied a capacity-based test, while Judge Kaul's dissent required State-like organisations). The ICTY didn't require policy (Kunarac).
Mental element: knowledge of the attack and that the conduct is part of it (not of all details). Motive is irrelevant.

Listed acts: murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation or forcible transfer, imprisonment, torture, sexual violence (rape, sexual slavery, enforced prostitution, forced pregnancy, enforced sterilisation), persecution, enforced disappearance, apartheid, and other inhumane acts.

Persecution (7(1)(h); 7(2)(g)): an intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights, contrary to IL, by reason of the identity of a group (political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious, gender, or other universally recognised grounds), in connection with another Art 7 act or crime under the Court's jurisdiction. Gender persecution is advancing: PTC II warrants of 8 July 2025 against Taliban leader Akhundzada and Chief Justice Haqqani (the first ICC gender-persecution warrants; 'gender' goes beyond biological sex; two more warrants Sept 2025, all unsealed 5 Oct 2026), while Al Hassan (2024) shows its limits: he was convicted of persecution on religious grounds, but the Chamber split on gender persecution, so there was no gender-persecution conviction. The concept of gender is debated (Art 7(3) definition dropped in the draft CAH convention).
Other inhumane acts (7(1)(k)): of a similar character, causing great suffering or serious injury, a residual category catching new harms. Forced marriage (AFRC Appeals SCSL; Ongwen ICC 2021).

Apartheid (7(2)(h)): inhumane acts in the context of an institutionalised regime of systematic oppression and domination by one racial group with the intention of maintaining that regime. Enforced disappearance (7(2)(i)).

Draft Articles on CAH (ILC 2019): GA Res 79/122 (4 Dec 2024) set the path to a convention: Preparatory Committee session 1 held 19–30 Jan 2026, session 2 on 12–15 Apr 2027, and a diplomatic conference in 2028 and 2029. The convention would cover prevention, punishment, and aut dedere aut judicare. This fills the gap, since there is no CAH treaty, unlike genocide and war crimes (Sadat).

Gender persecution update: the ICC unsealed (5 Oct 2026) two further Taliban warrants (Ministers Habibullah Agha and Neda Mohammad Nadim) alongside the July 2025 warrants for Akhundzada and Haqqani. PTC II held that 'gender' in Art 7(3) requires an interpretation beyond a purely biological conception of sex, and that gender persecution covers systemic, institutionalised harm such as discriminatory societal norms.

Enforced disappearance: Rome Art 7(2)(i) is narrower than the 2006 Convention (ICPPED Art 2). Rome adds an intent to remove the person from the protection of the law, 'for a prolonged period', and requires a State or 'political organization' plus a widespread or systematic attack. Under ICPPED a single case is a violation and only a widespread or systematic practice is a CAH (Art 5). Exam hook: is a cartel that counts as an 'organization' for the Art 7(2)(a) policy also a 'political organization' for Art 7(2)(i)? Burundi (PTC III, 2017) inferred the intent from the arbitrary manner of arrests.

Kress argues the structural difference between genocide and CAH is 'essentially technical': both are systemic crimes. In CAH the collective activity (the widespread or systematic attack) is an objective contextual element; in genocide it is the objective point of reference of the required intent. So in both, an initial act in an emerging campaign can be a completed crime (the Elements on 'initial acts in an emerging pattern' and on furthering an 'emerging' attack). Both definitions are drafted from the perspective of those who carry out the plan, not the leaders who direct it.

Policy element details from the Elements of Crimes (intro to Art 7, para 3 and fn 6): a policy requires that the State or organisation actively promote or encourage the attack. It may 'in exceptional circumstances' be implemented by a deliberate failure to act consciously aimed at encouraging the attack, but cannot be inferred solely from the absence of action. It need not be formally adopted and may be inferred from repetition, preparation or collective mobilisation (Katanga 2014); policy and 'systematic' are separate questions (Katanga; Gbagbo). Duterte (PTC I, Apr 2026): an organisational policy of the Davao Death Squad became a State policy during the presidency.
lecture: Notion (Heinsch): crimes committed on a massive scale against a civilian population. The typical case is mass murder, but there is no need to prove intent to destroy a whole group, and political and other groups are covered. Many modes: murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, torture, rape, enforced disappearance, apartheid.

IMT Art 6(c): murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation and other inhumane acts against any civilian population, before or during the war, or persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds, 'in execution of or in connection with' another IMT crime — a war nexus created for the Nazi crimes against Jews. Today no armed-conflict nexus exists.

ICTY Art 5 kept an armed conflict requirement as a jurisdictional limit only (Tadić 1995 para 141: custom requires no nexus); ICTR Art 3 required no armed conflict but did require discriminatory grounds for the attack (national, political, ethnic, racial, religious); individual discriminatory intent is needed only for persecution (Akayesu Appeal paras 464–469). In both: the act must form part of the attack and the perpetrator must know it (Kunarac Appeal paras 82–86, 99).

Structure under Rome Art 7: objective element = chapeau (widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population) plus a listed act; subjective element = intent and knowledge, including of the context.

Attack (Art 7(2)(a)): a course of conduct involving multiple commission of listed acts against a civilian population pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organisational policy. Not necessarily military; a single act by one perpetrator suffices if it is part of the overall attack.

Widespread is quantitative (victims, geography); systematic is qualitative (organised, improbable as random). Kunarac Appeal paras 90–100: alternatives; the attack as a whole must meet the threshold; the civilian population must be the primary target but need not be everyone in the area. Discussion: one killing of a civilian during a campaign of expulsions and killings can be a CAH.
Policy: no formal programme needed — planned, directed or organised as opposed to spontaneous, isolated acts; need not be explicit. Heinsch stresses it was originally not part of customary law.

Kenya (ICC PTC II, 31 March 2010, paras 84–93): an organisation need not be State-like; capacity matters — leadership, resources, ability to conduct a widespread or systematic attack — assessed case by case. Judge Kaul's dissent required State-like organisations. Note it was an authorisation decision at the 'reasonable basis' threshold. Discussion: could a powerful criminal cartel commit CAH? What facts would you need?

Listed acts, with the lecture's glosses: murder (unlawfully and intentionally causing death), extermination (killing on a large scale), enslavement (ownership of a person), deportation or forcible transfer ('ethnic cleansing'), imprisonment or other severe deprivation of liberty in violation of PIL (arbitrary), torture (no official-capacity requirement), sexual violence, persecution, enforced disappearance, apartheid, other inhumane acts.

cards.q: What are the five contextual elements of CAH (Rome Art 7)?
cards.a: (1) An attack, a course of conduct with multiple commission of acts; (2) directed against any civilian population; (3) widespread or systematic; (4) pursuant to a State or organisational policy; (5) the perpetrator's knowledge of the attack and that the conduct is part of it.

cards.q: What are the elements of persecution?
cards.a: A severe deprivation of fundamental rights contrary to IL; targeting a group or collectivity by reason of identity on prohibited grounds (including gender); in connection with another Art 7 act or ICC crime; discriminatory intent.

cards.q: What is the function of 'other inhumane acts'?
cards.a: A residual category for acts of similar character and gravity causing great suffering or serious injury to body or mental or physical health (e.g. forced marriage: AFRC, Ongwen). It must respect legality (nullum crimen).

cards.q: Why does a CAH convention matter?
cards.a: There is no treaty obliging States to prevent and punish CAH, unlike genocide (1948) and grave breaches (1949). The ILC draft would establish duties to prevent, criminalise, and extradite or prosecute, plus inter-State cooperation. The UNGA set negotiations for 2028–29.

cards.q: How would you charge Duterte's 'war on drugs'?
cards.a: As charged and confirmed (PTC I, 23 Apr 2026): three counts of murder and attempted murder as CAH (49 incidents, 78 victims), a widespread and systematic attack on a civilian population (alleged drug users and the urban poor) under State or organisational policy (speeches, the DDS, police quotas and rewards), with co-perpetration via a common plan. ICC jurisdiction covers 1 Nov 2011–16 Mar 2019 (Art 127(2), Appeals 22 Apr 2026). Trial from 30 Nov 2026.

cards.q: How did the nexus requirement for CAH evolve?
cards.a: IMT Art 6(c): connection with another IMT crime (war). CCL No. 10 dropped it. ICTY Art 5: armed conflict as a jurisdictional limit only (Tadić: custom needs no nexus). ICTR Art 3: no armed conflict, but discriminatory grounds for the attack. Rome Art 7: no armed conflict, no general discrimination requirement, but a State or organisational policy.

cards.q: Can a single killing be a CAH?
cards.a: Yes, if it forms part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population and the perpetrator knows this (Kunarac Appeal paras 90–100). The attack as a whole, not the individual act, must be widespread or systematic.

cards.q: What would reopening the CAH definition in the new convention risk, and what is proposed?
cards.a: Proposals: list forced marriage and gender apartheid as separate crimes, add the slave trade, starvation and reproductive violence; drop or keep the Art 7(3) gender definition; delete the persecution 'connection' requirement. Risks: some States want a cumulative 'widespread and systematic' chapeau, a link to armed conflict, immunity carve-outs, and they question jus cogens status. The Sixth Committee's consensus habit lets a few States block (Sadat 2024).

cards.q: Rome Art 7(2)(i) versus ICPPED: what extra does the CAH of enforced disappearance require?
cards.a: Intent to remove the person from the protection of the law for a prolonged period; a State or political organisation behind it (by, or with its authorisation, support or acquiescence); and the CAH chapeau (part of a widespread or systematic attack, with knowledge). ICPPED needs none of the intent or duration elements, and only State agents or those acting with State acquiescence; one case is enough for a violation.

topics.title: Genocide
core: Genocide Convention Art II (copied in Rome Art 6): acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: (a) killing members; (b) causing serious bodily or mental harm; (c) deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction; (d) imposing measures to prevent births; (e) forcibly transferring children.

It is both a crime for individuals (Art III punishable acts, including conspiracy, direct and public incitement, attempt, complicity) and a basis for State responsibility (Bosnia v Serbia: States are bound not to commit genocide, and have duties to prevent and punish, Art I).

Protected groups: four only (political and social groups excluded during the 1948 drafting, per Schabas). Akayesu's 'stable and permanent groups' extension has not been followed. Identification is through objective and subjective criteria (the perpetrator's perception, Jelisić; Stakić: positive, not negative, definition).

Dolus specialis: the intent to destroy the group as such, physical or biological destruction. Cultural genocide was excluded (Krstić; Bosnia para 344), though attacks on cultural property may evidence intent.
'In part': a substantial part, quantitatively or qualitatively significant (Krstić: the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, emblematic). It can be geographically limited (Bosnia para 199).

Proving intent: rarely direct, so it is inferred from circumstantial evidence. The ICJ still requires 'fully conclusive' evidence and 'the only reasonable inference' (Bosnia para 373; Croatia para 148), and Gambia v Myanmar (2026) kept both (paras 80, 438). But it REFINED the test. (1) It is a general test of international criminal law for circumstantial evidence (para 442). (2) Genocidal intent may coexist with other compatible intents such as displacement or punishment, and the test is met if 'the totality of the evidence can only be explained by the perpetrator's genocidal intent' even where some evidence allows other intentions (paras 443, 456, 464). (3) The respondent need not prove an alternative inference to a fully conclusive standard (para 450). (4) No prior 'pattern of conduct' finding is required; the Court weighs a non-exhaustive array of 'factors', including non-Art II conduct such as hate speech and discriminatory laws (paras 387-397). (5) A low death percentage is not decisive: compare with the targeted part and count all Art II victims (paras 429-430). This largely accepts the interveners' arguments (Canada and five others, the Maldives, Ireland, Slovenia, DRC, Belgium). The joint dissent of six judges says the standard was lowered in practice.

Kress's structural debate: individual intent versus a collective genocidal campaign (the Elements' 'manifest pattern of similar conduct' contextual element, ICC Al-Bashir). He criticises the ICJ in Bosnia v Serbia: it accepted collective genocidal intent only in theory, then examined the intent of unnamed individual perpetrators 'as though such intent could have existed in the absence of a collective genocidal act'. In his view the individual's genocidal intent normally presupposes knowledge of a collective genocidal campaign, without which there is only a 'vain genocidal hope'.

Divergence and fragmentation: ICTY and ICTR jurisprudence (Akayesu, the first conviction, rape as genocide; Krstić; Jelisić) versus the ICJ's stricter evidentiary approach (Bosnia: only Srebrenica, Serbia not responsible for commission). There is debate over whether the ICJ demands a higher 'fully conclusive' standard of proof.

ICJ genocide cases. Gambia v Myanmar was DECIDED on 19 Nov 2026 after merits hearings of 12-29 Jan 2026. By 9-6 Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine (2017 clearance operations), the first ICJ finding that a State itself committed genocide. It also breached the duties to prevent (9-6), to punish (11-4) and to legislate under Art V (14-1), and breached the 2020 provisional measure on preserving evidence (11-4). No incitement of private actors (14-1). Orders: legislate, investigate and prosecute, guarantees of non-repetition, restitution (return, property, rehabilitation, non-discrimination) and compensation to the Rohingya, with a report due within 2 years. Still pending: South Africa v Israel (provisional measures Jan, Mar and May 2024; Israel's Counter-Memorial, including jurisdictional objections, filed 12 Mar 2026; Reply due 22 Nov 2027, Rejoinder 22 May 2029); Ukraine v Russia (jurisdiction limited in 2024 to whether Ukraine committed genocide; Russia's counter-claims admitted Dec 2025); Nicaragua v Germany (hearings on preliminary objections Sept 2026).

Genocide in war: genocide can be committed in or outside armed conflict, and military objectives don't exclude genocidal intent (debate on dual intent). There is a relationship with CAH extermination and persecution (persecution versus genocide: discriminatory versus destructive intent).

Gambia v Myanmar (2026) on the elements. Rohingya = a distinct ethnic group on objective and subjective criteria (para 310). 'Destroy' is physical or biological but not limited to death: any Art II act, including serious mental harm, can destroy the group as such, and 'physical' appears only in Art II(c) (paras 289-293). Art II(c) 'calculated' is objective: conditions must be capable of causing the slow death of a substantial part, which was not proven (paras 345-356). Art II(d) was met by birth restrictions and sexual violence impairing procreation (paras 363-371). 'In part': about 815,000 northern Rakhine Rohingya, substantial on numbers alone (paras 379-380). IHL compliance may inform intent but does not exclude conduct from the Convention (para 305).

Gambia v Myanmar (2026) on the other obligations. PREVENT: breach is 'not conditioned on a finding that genocide has occurred', so a State cannot 'remain idle and gamble that the risk might not ultimately materialize' (para 487; a departure from Bosnia para 431 per Milanovic). PUNISH: an autonomous duty to investigate arises on 'reasonable grounds to suspect'; investigations must be prompt, effective, independent and impartial; prosecuting ordinary crimes is insufficient; Art IV includes command responsibility; destroying evidence and refusing to cooperate with UN mechanisms breaches Art VI (paras 513-554). ART V: genocide must be a distinct offence with genocidal intent and all Art III modes (paras 569-574). INCITEMENT: need not call for killing and may be coded, but must be a direct call to action (paras 499-506).

Schabas on ethnic cleansing: it is 'incorrect' to say ethnic cleansing is a form of genocide or even sometimes amounts to it. The material acts may look alike, but the specific intents differ, one to displace and one to destroy, and he thought it 'logically inconceivable' that the two agendas coexist. He adds that ethnic cleansing is a warning sign: genocide is 'the last resort of the frustrated ethnic cleanser'. The drafters deliberately excluded mass displacement (Syria's proposal was rejected). Contrast Gambia v Myanmar (2026, para 456): displacement and genocidal intent may coexist. A clear doctrinal shift to discuss.

Schabas on 'as such': the words were the Venezuelan compromise at the Sixth Committee. The UK wanted all reference to motive deleted; the USSR, Lebanon and others wanted listed motives. 'As such' was presented as reintroducing motive implicitly without listing it, though the US insisted the Committee did not necessarily adopt that reading. So whether genocide needs a motive (group membership as the reason) is not settled by the text. Today's courts treat motive as irrelevant to guilt, but the drafting history is ambiguous.

Schabas on the Convention's origins: genocide and CAH were 'forged in the same crucible' to describe Nazi crimes and used almost as synonyms at Nuremberg. The split arose only because the IMT tied CAH to the war, leaving peacetime atrocities unpunished, which prompted GA Res 96(I) (India, Cuba, Panama, days after the judgment). Had there been no nexus, 'there would have been no need to define genocide as a distinct international crime'. Now that CAH needs no nexus, the main legal consequence of the genocide label is ICJ access under Art IX; its weight is symbolic. Schwarzenberger: the Convention is 'unnecessary when applicable and inapplicable when necessary'.

Kress's knowledge-based approach to genocidal intent: it suffices that the perpetrator commits a prohibited act knowing that it furthers a campaign whose (realistic) goal is to destroy the group in whole or in part; personal desire for destruction is not required. His argument: the list of prohibited acts is drafted from the perspective of subordinates, while the dominant purpose-based approach imposes a leadership-level mens rea, which strains evidence and accessory liability. Eichmann and Arendt's 'banality of evil' show that executors often act without being 'personally imbued' with the collective aim. The purpose-based view remains dominant in the case law (Krstić, Jelisić).

Kress's critique of Srebrenica as genocide. First, treating the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica (about 40,000, roughly 2.9–3% of the group) as a 'part' lowers the quantitative threshold in a way that is hard to square with genocide's special stigma. Second, only 'part of a part' (the men) was killed and the rest expelled; calling lasting expulsion 'physical disappearance' reintroduces the rejected social concept of destruction 'through the backdoor' of 'in part'. A better route would have been Art II(d) (killing the men plus deporting the women as measures preventing births). In 2007 he faulted the ICJ for adopting Krstić without reasons, while praising it for rejecting Krstić's 'distinct entity' requirement and for limiting 'destroy' to physical or biological destruction. Its test of 'the area of the perpetrator's activity and control' wrongly uses the lone perpetrator as the yardstick.

Kress identifies three values protected by the crime: the survival of groups (Lemkin: a destroyed nation's lost 'future contributions to the world'; GA Res 96(I): 'great losses to humanity'), international peace and security, and the individual rights of victims on a massive scale. The perpetrator's view that individuals matter only as group members must not be confused with the law's protective aim.

Mazzeschi and Carli (on South Africa v Israel) defend the ICJ's high evidentiary bar: the 'only reasonable inference' test is correct 'by reason of the particular gravity of the crime', even if it approaches beyond reasonable doubt. Do not cite them as critics. They criticise applying the 'fully conclusive' standard to attribution as well. Their proposals: a State's genocidal intent is distinct from that of individual perpetrators (Bosnia separated the two but then examined both); for 'direct' State genocide the pattern of conduct should essentially be a widespread or systematic attack on a protected group; and the relevant intent is that of the Government acting collectively, identified through the primary rules of the Convention rather than ARSIWA attribution. Compare Gambia v Myanmar (2026), which inferred intent from the collective conduct of security forces and organs.
lecture: Origins: Lemkin (protecting minorities); not charged as such at Nuremberg; GA Res 96(I) (11 Dec 1946); Convention adopted 9 Dec 1948. Drafting fights: which groups, jurisdiction, cultural genocide, whether perpetrators must be officials, State responsibility.

Three key aspects: specific intent to destroy; a specific group; via an enumerated act involving physical or biological destruction. The 'intellectual divide': the legal concept (specific intent, four groups) versus the social concept (mass killing of any human group).

Dolus specialis (Mettraux): 'eminently specific and evidentially demanding' — an intent, to destroy, a group as such; two levels of special intent (the group as target, and its physical or biological destruction as the intended fate), on top of general intent for the underlying acts.

'Only reasonable inference': evidential narratives must be reduced to a single one that dispels any ambiguity. Questions raised: what counts as circumstantial evidence; when inference becomes proof; can intent be inferred from context in a military campaign (Croatia v Serbia, the Brioni transcripts, para 504); can intent exist without mass killing?

Pillay Commission (UN COI on the OPT) report, 16 Sept 2025 (A/HRC/60/CRP.3): intent may be shown by direct evidence (statements) or circumstantial evidence from the totality and pattern of conduct, including sexual and gender-based violence, acts against children, and conduct before, during and after (para 158); scale, systematic nature, casualties 'far in excess of military necessity' (para 159); other motives for discrete acts do not preclude genocidal intent if it is the only reasonable inference (para 160); officials' statements were received by forces as orders and executed (paras 162–163, 176); no military necessity justified the pattern (paras 177–179); destruction of cultural and religious sites is relevant to intent though not itself an Art II act (paras 188–189); denial of infant milk causing starvation of newborns is 'especially powerful evidence' (para 190).

'Destroy' means physical or biological destruction, not of identity (Kamuhanda para 627; Krstić: attacking cultural or sociological characteristics alone is not genocide). Blagojević (para 659): a group is also its history, traditions and relationships; a forcible transfer that prevents the group reconstituting itself can amount to destruction — genocide without killing. Popović (2010, para 824): forcible transfer alone is insufficient to infer intent to destroy (displacement is distinct), but it is relevant.
'In part': Krstić — the 7,500 Bosnian Muslim men of Srebrenica were a substantial part of the protected group.

Protected groups: political, economic and social groups were dropped in the Sixth Committee (opposed by China, the USSR and Poland as unstable) to save the international tribunal clause. No definitions in the Convention or travaux. Akayesu paras 512–515: national (a perceived legal bond of citizenship with reciprocal rights and duties), ethnic (shared language or culture), racial (hereditary physical traits linked to a region), religious (shared religion, denomination or worship). Semanza para 317: case by case, objective context plus perpetrators' subjective perceptions. Krstić paras 554–560: the four groups describe a single phenomenon, roughly 'national minorities'.

Update (after the lectures): Gambia v Myanmar, Judgment of 19 Nov 2026. The newly developed jurisprudence the lecturers asked students to cite covers the refined 'only reasonable inference' test (coexisting intents, totality of evidence: paras 442-443, 450, 456, 464), the factor-based inference of intent (paras 387-397), scale measured against the targeted part (paras 429-430), and prevention without genocide having occurred (para 487). On Kress's structural debate: the Court inferred the State's intent from the collective conduct of its security forces and organs, without identifying an individual 'mastermind' or a written plan.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Akayesu
cases.holding: The first international genocide conviction. Rape and sexual violence can constitute genocide (serious bodily or mental harm) when committed with intent to destroy. 'Stable and permanent groups' (not followed).
cases.use: Sexual violence as genocide; protected groups.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Krstić (Appeals)
cases.holding: The killing of Bosnian Muslim men at Srebrenica was genocide: the targeted part was substantial and emblematic of the whole group, and forcible transfer of women and children supported the inference. Krstić was guilty as an aider and abettor.
cases.use: 'In part'; substantiality; physical destruction.

cases.name: Bosnia v Serbia (Genocide)
cases.holding: States can be responsible for genocide. Srebrenica was genocide, but not attributable to Serbia. Serbia breached its duty to prevent (capacity to influence) and to punish. Intent must be the only reasonable inference from a pattern of conduct.
cases.use: State responsibility; prevention; the evidentiary standard.

cases.name: Croatia v Serbia
cases.holding: Both claims were rejected. The actus reus was established for some acts, but the intent to destroy was not the only reasonable inference (the aim was forced displacement).
cases.use: The difficulty of proving dolus specialis.

cases.name: South Africa v Israel (provisional measures)
cases.holding: The rights of Palestinians in Gaza to protection from acts of genocide are plausible. Israel was ordered to prevent genocidal acts and incitement, enable humanitarian aid, and (May 2024) halt its military offensive in Rafah in so far as it may inflict destructive conditions of life.
cases.use: The plausibility standard; current debates on intent (Mazzeschi and Carli).

cases.name: Prosecutor v Blagojević and Jokić
cases.holding: Physical or biological destruction is not necessarily the death of group members; a forcible transfer conducted so the group cannot reconstitute itself, especially by separating members, can lead to material destruction (Trial Chamber, para 659). Note: on appeal (2007) Blagojević's conviction for complicity in genocide was quashed, so para 659 is a Trial Chamber dictum; contrast Popović para 824.
cases.use: Genocide without killing; the meaning of 'destroy'.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Popović et al.
cases.holding: Forcible transfer alone is an insufficient basis to infer intent to destroy, because intent to displace differs from intent to destroy, but it is relevant in assessing genocidal intent (para 824).
cases.use: Ethnic cleansing versus genocide.

cases.name: UN Commission of Inquiry on the OPT (Pillay Commission) report
cases.holding: Found genocidal intent in Gaza from officials' statements (direct evidence) and the pattern of conduct (circumstantial), holding that alternative military aims for discrete acts do not exclude genocidal intent where it is the only reasonable inference from the totality of evidence.
cases.use: Applying the only-reasonable-inference test in war (lecture's main case study).

cases.name: The Gambia v Myanmar (Application of the Genocide Convention), Merits
cases.holding: By 9-6, Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine (2017 clearance operations): killing, serious bodily and mental harm, and measures to prevent births, with intent to destroy a substantial part. The 'only reasonable inference' test was retained but met because intent explains the totality of the evidence; counter-insurgency, forcible displacement and punishment were rejected as alternative reasonable inferences (paras 438-467). Also breaches of prevent (9-6), punish (11-4), Art V (14-1) and provisional measure 3 (11-4); no incitement of private actors (14-1). Restitution and compensation are owed to the Rohingya as a group and as individuals, claimable by a non-injured State (paras 585-625).
cases.use: The leading authority on proving State genocidal intent (coexisting intents, totality of evidence, factors); duty to prevent without genocide having occurred; duty to investigate; erga omnes partes reparation. Contrast Bosnia (2007) and Croatia (2015).

cards.q: What are the elements of genocide?
cards.a: Actus reus: one of the five Art II acts against members of a protected group (national, ethnical, racial, religious). Mens rea: general intent for the act, plus specific intent (dolus specialis) to destroy the group, in whole or in part, as such.

cards.q: What is the 'only reasonable inference' standard?
cards.a: When intent is inferred from circumstantial evidence, genocidal intent must be the only reasonable inference (Bosnia para 373; Croatia para 148). Gambia v Myanmar (2026, paras 442-443) kept the test but clarified it. It is a general ICL test; genocidal intent may coexist with other compatible intents; and it is met when 'the totality of the evidence can only be explained by the perpetrator's genocidal intent', even if some evidence allows other intentions. Critics, including the six-judge joint dissent, say it was applied more loosely than in Croatia.

cards.q: What does 'in part' mean in Krstić?
cards.a: A substantial part of the group, judged by numerical size relative to the whole, prominence and emblematic significance, and the perpetrator's area of activity and control (the last factor is contested: Kress 2007, p 627, criticises it as letting a geographically limited 'part of a part' qualify). A geographically limited part can qualify.

cards.q: Persecution versus genocide?
cards.a: Both are discriminatory. Persecution (CAH) aims at deprivation of rights on prohibited grounds. Genocide requires intent to physically or biologically destroy the group. Persecution is 'the genus', genocide the extreme form (Kupreškić).

cards.q: What duties do States have under Art I of the Genocide Convention?
cards.a: To prevent (due diligence, triggered once the State learns or should have learned of a serious risk; measured by capacity to influence) and to punish (prosecute, cooperate with competent international tribunals). Also the implied obligation not to commit genocide (Bosnia).

cards.q: What are Akayesu's definitions of the four protected groups?
cards.a: National: a perceived legal bond of common citizenship with reciprocal rights and duties (para 512). Ethnic: a shared language or culture (513). Racial: hereditary physical traits often linked to a region (514). Religious: a shared religion, denomination or mode of worship (515). Later case law adds a subjective element (Semanza para 317).

cards.q: Can genocide be committed without killing?
cards.a: Yes. Art II(b)–(e) acts suffice with the specific intent; and Blagojević held a forcible transfer preventing the group from reconstituting itself can amount to destruction. But Popović: forcible transfer alone does not prove intent to destroy.

cards.q: How did the Pillay Commission (2025) handle military-necessity arguments?
cards.a: Other motives for discrete acts (military advantage, destroying an armed group) do not preclude genocidal intent if it remains the only reasonable inference from the totality of evidence; it found casualties far in excess of military necessity and no military necessity justifying the pattern (paras 159–160, 177–179).

cards.q: Which factors did the ICJ use to infer Myanmar's genocidal intent (Gambia v Myanmar 2026, para 397)?
cards.a: (a) General context and other culpable acts: discriminatory laws and citizenship denial, Tatmadaw-organised hate speech, earlier operations, forcible displacement. (b) Selective targeting of the Rohingya, with burning of villages and resettlement of non-Rohingya. (c) Acts violating the group's foundations: sexual violence, targeting of children. (d) Systematic nature and scale. No prior pattern-of-conduct finding was required, and the factors are non-exhaustive (paras 387, 396).

cards.q: How did Gambia v Myanmar distinguish genocide from ethnic cleansing?
cards.a: Forcible displacement is not genocide as such but can support an inference of intent (para 407). Displacement and genocidal intent may coexist (para 456). Unlike Bosnia and Croatia, there was no transfer or evacuation plan, and the security forces shot, mined and sank boats of fleeing Rohingya, burned villages so there was nothing to return to, and killed children. Displacement therefore did not explain the totality of the evidence (paras 457-462).

cards.q: Does breach of the duty to prevent genocide require that genocide occurred?
cards.a: No, according to Gambia v Myanmar 2026, para 487: responsibility 'is not conditioned on a finding that genocide has occurred', and a State may not 'gamble that the risk might not ultimately materialize'. The duty is triggered by a serious risk, including a risk of genocidal intent (para 479). This departs from Bosnia para 431 (Milanovic). Myanmar breached it by failing to restrain non-Rohingya civilians who joined the clearance operations (para 488).

cards.q: What does the duty to punish require after Gambia v Myanmar?
cards.a: To investigate (an autonomous, due-diligence duty triggered by reasonable grounds to suspect), to prosecute and to punish, including commanders (superior responsibility is read into Art IV), before a competent and impartial tribunal with effective penalties. Prosecution for ordinary crimes without genocidal intent does not suffice. Under Art VI the State must either prosecute or cooperate with an international penal tribunal. Destroying evidence breaches the duty (paras 513-554).

cards.q: Schabas versus Gambia v Myanmar on ethnic cleansing and genocide?
cards.a: Schabas (2000): displacement and destruction are different specific intents and cannot logically coexist, so ethnic cleansing is never genocide, though it may be its 'warning sign'. ICJ (Gambia v Myanmar 2026, paras 407, 456–462): forcible displacement is not genocide as such and can support an inference of intent; displacement and genocidal intent may coexist, and here displacement could not explain the totality of the evidence (boats sunk, villages burned, children killed).

cards.q: What are Mazzeschi and Carli's three proposals on proving State genocidal intent?
cards.a: (1) State intent is distinct from individual intent; (2) the relevant pattern of conduct for 'direct' State genocide is essentially a widespread or systematic attack on the protected group; (3) the intent that counts is the Government's, as a collective executive, under the Convention's primary rules rather than ARSIWA. They support the 'only reasonable inference' threshold as correct given the gravity, but reject applying 'fully conclusive' proof to attribution.

cards.q: Knowledge-based versus purpose-based genocidal intent?
cards.a: Purpose-based (dominant case law: Akayesu, Krstić, Jelisić): the perpetrator must aim at the group's destruction. Knowledge-based (Kress, after Greenawalt): it suffices to commit a listed act knowing it furthers a collective campaign realistically aimed at destruction. Kress: the actus reus list targets subordinates, so a leadership-level 'purpose' requirement mismatches the definition; Eichmann's 'banality of evil'.

cards.q: Why does Schabas say genocide and CAH were 'forged in the same crucible'?
cards.a: Both described the Nazi crimes and were near-synonyms in 1945. The IMT's war nexus for CAH left peacetime atrocities unpunished, so GA Res 96(I) and the 1948 Convention created genocide as a separate crime. With the nexus gone, the main legal difference is ICJ access under Art IX; the rest is symbolic (Bosnians and Darfur victims disappointed by 'only' CAH). Schwarzenberger: 'unnecessary when applicable and inapplicable when necessary'.

excerpts.cite: ICJ Merits (19 Nov 2026), para 646(1), by 9 votes to 6
excerpts.text: Finds that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide;
excerpts.why: The first ICJ finding that a State itself committed genocide. Against: Sebutinde, Tomka, Abraham, Xue, Nolte and judge ad hoc Kress.

excerpts.text: …the Court will base its assessment of the existence of genocidal intent in the present case on the following factors: (a) the general context, including the perpetration of other culpable acts systematically directed against the Rohingya; (b) the selective targeting of the Rohingya; (c) the perpetration of acts that violate the foundations of the Rohingya group; and (d) the systematic nature and the scale of Myanmar's actions.
excerpts.why: A four-factor framework for inferring intent; use it to structure a problem answer.

excerpts.text: …genocidal intent may exist alongside other intentions, provided that such intentions are not incompatible with the existence of genocidal intent… When some elements of the evidentiary record may allow additional intentions to be inferred, but the totality of the evidence can only be explained by the perpetrator's genocidal intent, the only reasonable inference standard is met.
excerpts.why: The refined 'only reasonable inference' test: coexisting intents (displacement, counter-insurgency) no longer defeat the inference (see also para 456).

excerpts.text: …the obligation to prevent genocide does not allow a State that is in a position to act in the face of a serious risk of genocide to remain idle and gamble that the risk might not ultimately materialize… international responsibility for breach of the duty to prevent genocide is not conditioned on a finding that genocide has occurred.
excerpts.why: A departure from Bosnia para 431; criticised by Judges Tomka, Nolte and Abraham.

excerpts.text: …genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such…
excerpts.why: The protected groups, the five acts and the dolus specialis.
